# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Teral Plain Array Muon/Electromagnetic Separation

## 1. What limits the array today

- **No separation in the signal.** Each water tank gives one light trace in which muons and electromagnetic (EM) particles are mixed. Muon number can only be inferred statistically from trace shape (rise time, "jumps"). That gives only loose per-event constraints, nowhere near 30%.
- **Showers are near-vertical.** At 0–35° zenith, the EM component is still large at the ground, typically comparable to or larger than the muonic signal at 500–1000 m from the core. A separation method must work where the EM component is strong. This rules out inclined-shower tricks.
- **The tanks cannot be modified inside.** They are closed, one-piece vessels filled to within 5 cm of the lid. Internal changes, such as a reflective divider to make a two-layer tank, would mean draining and cutting 1,350 sealed vessels in the field. That is impractical, so new detector elements must be added outside the tank.
- **The site helps.** It is high, dry grassland with soil suitable for burial and a dense 0.7 km grid. At 10^19.5 eV, many stations lie within about 1 km of the core, so muon density can be sampled at several distances.

## 2. Proposed upgrades, in priority order

### A. Buried muon counter at every station (primary upgrade)

- **Design:** segmented plastic scintillator modules, about 20–30 m² per station.
  - Buried at about 2.3 m depth, which is roughly 540 g/cm² of soil.
  - Placed beside the tank, offset a few metres so the tank does not shadow them.
- **Why it works:** the soil absorbs essentially all of the EM component. The modules see muons above about 1 GeV almost cleanly, which gives a direct muon count independent of the tank.
- **Readout:**
  - Fine segmentation, about 64 strips per module, with wavelength-shifting fibres to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs).
  - Counting mode: number of strips hit within a time window.
  - Integrator mode: total charge, for high densities near the core where counting saturates.
- **Statistics check:**
  - Muon density at 10^19.5 eV around 800–1000 m is about 1–2 per m².
  - A 30 m² module therefore records tens of muons per station.
  - Several such stations per event make a muon-number resolution well below 30% achievable. Most of the remaining spread comes from shower-to-shower physics rather than counting.
- **Power and cost:**
  - SiPM readout keeps power low, a few watts, within the existing solar budget.
  - The soil overburden also stabilises temperature.
  - This is the costliest item (excavation plus plastic). If funds force phasing, equip an infill subset first. Full coverage is what the "every event" requirement implies.

### B. Surface scintillator on each tank lid (strongly recommended companion)

- **Design:** a scintillator panel of about 4 m², 1 cm thick, under a weatherproof aluminium roof, mounted on a frame over the lid.
- **Why it works:** the panel and the 1.3 m of water (about 3.6 radiation lengths) respond very differently to EM particles and muons:
  - The thin scintillator sees EM particles and muons roughly equally, by particle count.
  - The water tank is dominated by EM energy deposit plus muon track length.
  - Combining the two signals separates the EM and muonic components at each station, for every station. This works best at low zenith, which matches the 0–35° programme.
- **Value:**
  - Gives a second, independent muon estimate.
  - Gives a cleaner EM measurement that is itself sensitive to the depth of shower maximum (Xmax).
  - Lets the buried counters be cross-calibrated against the surface measurement.
- **Cost:** much cheaper and quicker to deploy than burial.

### C. Station electronics replacement (required by A and B)

- New digitiser board with:
  - faster sampling (about 120 MHz or more);
  - more channels to serve the tank, lid scintillator and buried counter;
  - improved timing for the satellite time stamp;
  - more on-board processing for local triggers and data compression over the existing radio link.

### D. Small photomultiplier for dynamic range

- Add a small photomultiplier in each tank, and a matching high/low-gain split on the scintillator readout.
- This avoids saturation near the core. At 10^19.5 eV and above, the stations nearest the core saturate and would otherwise be lost to the muon fit.
- Installing it requires access through the tank's existing photomultiplier ports. It is a modest intervention compared with internal segmentation.

### E. Calibration using fluorescence-detector "hybrid" events (operations, not new hardware)

- Use the 12% of events also seen by the fluorescence sites, where Xmax is measured directly.
- Use them to calibrate the muon-number and EM estimators and to validate the 30% resolution target.

## 3. Options not recommended

- **Radio antennas:** useful mainly for inclined showers and measure the EM component, so they add little muon information at 0–35°.
- **Internal tank segmentation (two-layer tank):** physically effective, but incompatible with the sealed, nearly full vessels.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a buried (~2.3 m deep), segmented ~20–30 m² scintillator muon counter with SiPM readout at every station, with lid-mounted surface scintillators as a companion.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Teral Plain Array: Separating Muons from the Electromagnetic Signal

## The core problem

Each station records one mixed light signal from 0.25 m of water. That signal cannot be split into muons and electromagnetic (EM) particles, for three reasons:

- **Muons and EM particles look alike in shallow water.** A vertical muon crossing 0.25 m deposits only about 55 MeV. That is not much more than an absorbed electron or photon of tens of MeV, which is the typical EM particle at 1 km from the core.
- **Photon conversion is incomplete and variable.** The water is only about 0.7 radiation lengths deep, so photons convert unevenly. The muon-to-EM signal ratio is therefore small and noisy.
- **The composition zenith band (0–35°) is the worst case.** Near-vertical showers are the most EM-dominated, and muon tracks there are shortest. Pulse-shape and "jump" methods that work for inclined showers do not work here.

So the array needs a second, physically different measurement at every station. Software alone will not reach 30% muon-number resolution.

## Proposed upgrades, in priority order

### 1. A buried, segmented muon counter at every station (direct muon measurement)

**Shielding**
- Place a scintillator module beside each tank, buried about 2.3 m deep (roughly 540 g/cm² of soil).
- This absorbs essentially all of the EM component. Only muons above about 1 GeV get through.
- This works for vertical showers, unlike any surface-only method.

**Detector**
- About 30 m² per station, built as 2–3 modules of 10 m².
- Each module holds 64 extruded polystyrene scintillator strips (about 4 m × 4 cm × 1 cm).
- Light is collected by wavelength-shifting fibres and read out by silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays, which are low-power, rugged and solar-compatible.

**Counting mode**
- Fine segmentation lets the counter count individual muons in a binary/counting mode.
- An integrator channel extends the range to high densities near the shower core.
- A statistical correction handles pile-up of muons in the same strip.

**Why this meets the 30% requirement**
- At 10^19.5 eV, the muon density near 1 km from the core is of order 1–few per m².
- A 30 m² counter at each of several stations near that distance gives tens of muons per counter. That keeps the Poisson error well under 30%.
- Fitting the lateral distribution across 3–6 stations sets the event-level muon number.
- Detector systematics are set by the counting method, not by a model of the tank.

**Burial practicalities**
- Trenching or "mole" installation is feasible on dry, high grassland.
- Each counter needs a soil-density survey to fix its overburden.

### 2. A scintillator slab on each tank lid (EM-weighted second response)

- Mount a 2–4 m², 1 cm thick plastic scintillator (WLS fibres, one PMT or SiPM) above the tank lid, under a sun-proof roof.
- It responds to particle count, so it is EM-dominated. The tank responds to deposited energy, which includes muons.
- Taking the scintillator and water signals together gives a cross-check of the EM component and of the buried counter's calibration. It also gives an EM-energy estimator at every station.

### 3. Deepen the water to about 1.2 m

- Replace or refit the vessels to hold about 1.2 m of water.
- This makes the tank more calorimetric for photons and raises the muon track signal to about 240 MeV.
- The tank-versus-scintillator contrast then becomes usable rather than nearly degenerate.
- This is the expensive, optional step. It mainly helps the surface-only analysis and the treatment of stations near the core.

### 4. Electronics and dynamic range

- **New station digitiser:** 120 MHz, 12-bit FADCs with more channels, to read the tank PMTs, the scintillator and the buried counter together.
- **Event-by-event timing:** better GPS timing (about 5 ns) and common triggering across all three detectors.
- **Small-area PMT (about 1 inch) in each tank:** extends dynamic range by about 30× so stations near the core do not saturate.
- **Larger solar panel and battery,** since the buried and lid detectors add load.

### 5. Optional: a radio antenna per station

- Add dual-polarisation antennas (30–80 MHz) at each station.
- These give a full-duty-cycle measurement of EM energy, and a modest Xmax sensitivity, that is independent of the water signal.
- This sharpens the muon-number-versus-EM ratio used for composition.

### Calibration

- Use the fluorescence sites' 12% hybrid events to cross-calibrate muon number against Xmax and energy.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a ~30 m² buried (~2.3 m soil-shielded), fibre/SiPM-read segmented scintillator muon counter at every station to count muons directly.

# AugerPrime-style Upgrade Recommendation for the Pierre Auger Surface Detector

## The core problem

Each water-Cherenkov detector (WCD) records one signal. In that signal, electrons and photons (EM) and muons are mixed. The muon number and the EM/muon ratio carry most of the mass information. Iron showers have about 40% more muons than proton showers and an earlier X_max. To recover mass event by event, each station needs a second measurement whose response to EM particles and to muons differs strongly from the WCD's.

The constraints rule out several options:
- **No opening the tank.** This excludes internal segmentation, a second water layer, or new PMTs inside the liner.
- **No lifting or relocating.** This excludes slab detectors placed under the tank.
- **Budget and labour.** Roughly US$6.2k and 5.8 person-hours per station require a preassembled, bolt-on unit that a two-person crew can install from a pickup.

## Recommendations

### 1. Surface Scintillator Detector (SSD) on the tank lid (highest priority)

**Design**
- About 3.8 m² of extruded polystyrene scintillator: 48 bars, each 1.6 m × 5 cm × 1 cm, made with the Fermilab co-extrusion process.
- Each bar is read by wavelength-shifting fibres (Kuraray Y-11) routed to a single 1.5-inch PMT (e.g. Hamamatsu R9420).
- The PMT is read out on two gain channels to cover dynamic range from one MIP to over 20,000 particles.
- The detector sits in a light-tight aluminium enclosure on a galvanised steel frame that clamps to the tank's existing lifting lugs.
- A sun-roof shields it from thermal swings.

**Why it works**
- A thin scintillator responds about equally per particle to EM particles and muons.
- The 1.2 m water volume responds far more strongly to muons, which cross the full depth, than to the EM component, which is largely absorbed.
- With two detectors of different response at the same location, a 2×2 inversion gives separate EM and muon signals at each station.
- From these one can derive N_μ and the EM-to-muon ratio at 1000 m, which give event-by-event mass sensitivity below 60°.
- This is most effective at high energy (above 10^19.5 eV), where many stations are hit.

**Why it fits the constraints**
- The tank interior is untouched, so the WCD response stays identical to the archive.
- Units are factory-built and tested, and two fit on a pickup.
- Installation takes about 3–4 person-hours: place the frame, lift on the module (light, about 150 kg), run the cable.
- Estimated cost is about US$2.5–3k per station.

### 2. Upgraded station electronics (UUB)

**Design**
- Replace the external electronics box, which is outside the sealed volume.
- New digitisers: 120 MHz, 12-bit ADCs instead of 40 MHz, 10-bit.
- A modern FPGA with a processor (Xilinx Zynq).
- Inputs for the SSD and extra channels.
- An improved GPS receiver for timing near 5 ns.
- More flexible triggers.

**Justification**
- The SSD needs to be read out and timed together with the WCD; the existing electronics cannot do this.
- The faster sampling resolves muon spikes against the smooth EM trace in the WCD. This gives an independent muon estimate and improves X_max reconstruction from rise time with machine-learning methods.
- The higher dynamic range reduces saturation near the shower core. The existing PMT anode and dynode outputs are kept, with no change to the PMTs themselves.
- Backward-compatible firmware can emulate the legacy triggers and response, preserving continuity with the archived data.

**Cost and labour:** about US$2k per station and about 1 person-hour to swap the box.

### 3. Deployment logistics and calibration (within the remaining budget, about US$1–1.5k per station)

- Spares, cabling, and a solar panel or battery upgrade to cover the additional power load.
- Calibration of every SSD with atmospheric muons in situ, using MIP peaks recorded through the UUB.
- Total labour stays under 5.8 person-hours per station.

## Considered and rejected or deferred

| Option | Decision | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Buried muon counters (scintillators at about 2.3 m depth) | Not array-wide | Excavation is far beyond 5.8 person-hours and the cost envelope. Worth considering only as a small infill cross-calibration subarray. |
| Scintillators or RPCs beneath the tank | Rejected | Requires lifting 12 t tanks. |
| Small PMT inside the liner, or a segmented-water upgrade | Rejected | Requires opening the sealed volume. |
| Radio antennas (e.g. SALLA) | Deferred | Most powerful for zenith angles above 60°, which is outside this goal's range. |

## Summary

SSD plus UUB gives each of the 1,660 stations an independent EM/muon separation at 100% duty cycle. The total is about US$6k per station and about 5 person-hours, with the original WCD response untouched.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a ~3.8 m² plastic-scintillator Surface Scintillator Detector (with WLS-fibre/PMT readout) on top of every water-Cherenkov tank to separate the electromagnetic and muonic signals.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Teral Plain Array

## Context and Constraints

The core problem is separating muonic from electromagnetic (EM) components in a water-Cherenkov array where both are mixed in a single signal. The 80–84° zenith angle strategy (highly inclined showers) already exploits the fact that EM component is attenuated at large zenith angles, but resolution is still marginal. The upgrades below address this directly.

---

## 1. Segmented Underground Muon Counters (Highest Priority)

**Technology:** Scintillator panels (plastic scintillator tiles, e.g., EJ-200 or similar) buried ~2.5 m underground beneath a subset (~25–30%) of existing stations, each covering ~3–4 m².

**Specifics:**
- Plastic scintillator slabs (1 cm thick, ~1.5 m × 2 m panels) read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs, e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or OnSemi MicroFB)
- Burial depth of 2.5 m of soil (~540 g/cm² overburden) suppresses EM component by factor ~10⁶, leaving a nearly pure muon signal
- SiPMs preferred over traditional PMTs: no high voltage supply, lower power draw (critical for solar-powered autonomous stations), radiation-hard, operable over wide temperature range (important for high grassland environment)
- Each underground unit communicates via the existing radio link with minor firmware additions
- A sparse deployment at every 4th station (≈340 underground counters) provides sufficient lateral sampling for muon lateral distribution function (LDF) fitting

**Expected improvement:** Direct muon counting reduces muon number resolution from ~30% to ~15% at 10^19.5 eV, breaking the EM/muon degeneracy without relying on zenith angle tricks.

---

## 2. Segmentation of Existing Water-Cherenkov Stations

**Technology:** Installation of a horizontal segmentation layer inside existing vessels using a thin (3 mm) HDPE or Tyvek-lined floating partition at ~0.5 m depth, creating a shallow upper layer and a deep lower layer, each read by one of the existing PMTs.

**Specifics:**
- The shallow layer (~0.5 m water) is predominantly sensitive to EM particles (short radiation length in water, ~36 g/cm²); muons deposit minimum-ionizing energy through both layers
- The deep layer (~0.8 m) gives a signal weighted toward muons relative to the shallow layer
- The ratio of deep-to-shallow signals provides an EM/muon discriminant event-by-event without added hardware cost beyond the partition
- Partition material: UV-stabilized Tyvek 1082D (already standard in Cherenkov detector liners) sealed to vessel inner walls with waterproof polyethylene welding
- Requires re-calibration of both PMT channels; existing electronics can handle two-channel readout
- This is a low-cost retrofit executable during scheduled station maintenance

**Expected improvement:** Provides ~20–25% muon fraction estimation per station, improving overall shower muon number resolution when combined with LDF fitting across the array.

---

## 3. Upgraded PMT Electronics with Waveform Digitization

**Technology:** Replace existing charge-integrating ADC front-end boards with FADC (flash ADC) waveform digitizers at 120 MSPS, 12-bit resolution.

**Specifics:**
- Current single light signal integration conflates the sharp, early muon Cherenkov pulses (ns-scale rise) with the broader, delayed EM cascade signals
- FADCs (e.g., based on DRS4 chip from PSI, or custom FPGA-based design using Xilinx Artix-7) digitize full waveform at 120 MHz, allowing pulse shape discrimination
- Muon signals in water Cherenkov detectors produce sharper, narrower pulses than EM shower particles; risetime discrimination can separate components statistically on a signal-by-signal basis
- Each FADC board consumes ~1.5 W additional power; feasible with modest solar panel upgrade (see item 5)
- On-board FPGA performs pulse-finding and compression before radio transmission; raw waveform storage is local (8 GB SD card, overwritten on 72-hour cycle) for post-event retrieval via triggered download

**Expected improvement:** Pulse-shape analysis on highly inclined showers (80–84°) where muon front arrives earlier than residual EM provides ~10–15% additional muon number resolution improvement on top of hardware segmentation.

---

## 4. Radio Emission Detection Add-On (Sparse Deployment)

**Technology:** Dual-polarization broadband radio antennas (30–80 MHz band, similar to AERA at Auger or LOFAR low band) at every 9th station (~150 antenna positions, ~1.6 km spacing).

**Specifics:**
- Butterfly or bow-tie dipole antennas at 2 m height, oriented N-S and E-W
- Low-noise amplifiers (LNA, noise figure <1 dB, e.g., based on BFP740 transistor used in AERA)
- Digitized at 200 MSPS with 12-bit ADC (similar to Auger's AERA electronics)
- Radio signal from extensive air showers is dominated by geomagnetic emission (proportional to EM content) with a subdominant charge-excess term; together these constrain X_max and EM energy independently of fluorescence
- Critically, radio works 100% of the time (unlike fluorescence at 12%), providing X_max-correlated mass proxy at full duty cycle
- At 1.6 km spacing the radio footprint for 10^19 eV showers (Cherenkov ring radius ~200 m at shower max) is adequately sampled for inclined showers where the footprint is elliptically stretched

**Expected improvement:** Radio X_max resolution of ~20 g/cm² for inclined showers gives full-time EM shower profile information, allowing cross-calibration of the muon-based composition estimator across the entire dataset rather than just the 12% fluorescence-visible fraction.

---

## 5. Solar Power and Communication Infrastructure Upgrade

**Technology:** Increase per-station solar panel capacity from (assumed) ~10 W to 25 W using monocrystalline panels (e.g., SunPower Maxeon 3, 22.8% efficiency), and replace satellite timing with White Rabbit protocol over a fiber backbone at hub nodes.

**Specifics:**
- Additional ~15 W per station accommodates FADC boards and underground scintillator electronics
- LiFePO₄ battery chemistry (replacing lead-acid if currently used): higher cycle life (>3000 cycles), better low-temperature performance at high-altitude grassland sites (down to −20°C), safer chemistry
- White Rabbit timing: GPS-disciplined fiber network between hub nodes (every ~5 km) achieves <1 ns synchronization accuracy vs. ~10–20 ns for typical GPS-only systems; critical for waveform-level timing used in muon front arrival analysis
- Radio link upgrade from narrowband to 802.11ah (Wi-Fi HaLow, 900 MHz band) for increased bandwidth needed for waveform data transfer

---

## 6. Atmospheric Monitoring Enhancement

**Technology:** Deploy a network of 6 aerosol LIDAR units (elastic backscatter LIDAR at 355 nm) at the fluorescence sites plus 4 intermediate positions, supplemented by 20 autonomous cloud cameras (all-sky fish-eye, IR-sensitive).

**Specifics:**
- LIDAR units based on Nd:YAG frequency-tripled lasers (355 nm, 50 mJ/pulse, 10 Hz), fiber-coupled to 30 cm Cassegrain receivers
- Provide aerosol optical depth profiles in real-time, reducing systematic uncertainty on fluorescence X_max from ~15 g/cm² to ~5 g/cm²
- Cloud cameras use uncooled microbolometer arrays (e.g., FLIR Lepton) for 24/7 cloud fraction monitoring, allowing better selection of fluorescence-quality nights and improving the 12% duty cycle estimate
- This directly improves the fluorescence cross-calibration of the array-based composition estimator

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Cost Level | Impact on Muon Resolution | Duty Cycle Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Underground scintillator counters | High | ★★★★★ | 100% |
| Station segmentation (Tyvek partition) | Low | ★★★ | 100% |
| FADC waveform digitization | Medium | ★★★ | 100% |
| Sparse radio array | Medium | ★★★★ | 100% |
| Power/timing upgrade | Medium | Enabling | 100% |
| Atmospheric LIDAR/cameras | Medium | ★★ (systematic) | Improves 12% |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Deploy plastic scintillator muon counters with SiPM readout buried at 2.5 m depth beneath ~25% of stations, providing a direct, nearly pure muon signal that immediately breaks the EM/muon degeneracy and brings muon number resolution well below the 30% requirement at full 100% duty cycle.

# Hardware upgrades for mass-sensitive surface-array operation above 10^19.5 eV

**Core problem:** each tank gives one mixed signal. To get proton/iron sensitivity at 100% duty cycle, each station needs a second measurement with a different electromagnetic-to-muon response. Combining the two responses separates the two shower components event by event (the muon number tracks the primary mass), and it also improves Xmax estimates. The tanks cannot be opened, lifted or moved, so any new detector must be external and added without disturbing them.

## 1. Surface Scintillator Detector (SSD) on each tank roof (the key upgrade)

**Technology**
- About 3.8 m² of extruded plastic scintillator bars (roughly 1.6 m × 5 cm × 1 cm).
- Bars are co-extruded with a TiO₂ reflective coating.
- Wavelength-shifting fibres are routed in grooves and bundled to one 1.5-inch PMT.
- The PMT is read out at two gains (anode and amplified dynode), giving dynamic range from single particles to near-core densities.
- The module sits in a light-tight aluminium enclosure on a steel or aluminium frame bolted onto the tank roof. A sun-roof shields it from temperature swings.

**Why this technology**
- A thin scintillator responds mainly to the electromagnetic component, while the 1.2 m water volume responds strongly to muons. The different response matrices let the electromagnetic and muon signals be unfolded at every station.
- It meets every constraint:
  - The sealed water volume, liner and PMTs are untouched, so the archived station response is preserved.
  - Nothing is lifted or drained.
  - Mass-produced extruded scintillator, as used for MINERvA, fits the roughly US$6,200 per-station budget.
  - A pre-assembled module can be delivered by pickup or flatbed and mounted by a 2–3 person crew in about 2 hours, within the 5.8 person-hour allowance.
- Its response is well matched to zenith angles below 60°. At larger angles its sensitivity falls, which is acceptable for this physics goal.

## 2. Upgraded station electronics (new unified board replacing the old one)

**Technology**
- Sampling rate raised from 40 to 120 MHz, with 12-bit flash ADCs (previously 10-bit).
- Extra input channels for the SSD PMT.
- A more powerful FPGA and CPU for new triggers, such as time-over-threshold and multiplicity-of-positive-steps triggers that are sensitive to muon-like pulses.
- A modern GPS receiver with better timing accuracy (a few ns).
- Expanded monitoring, with slots for future detectors.

**Why**
- Faster, finer sampling resolves individual muon spikes in the water trace. This allows muon counting and better signal rise-time and shape analysis, which also carry mass information.
- More bits and the dual-gain readout reduce saturation near the shower core. A small extra PMT inside the tank would also help with saturation, but it is excluded because the tank may not be opened.
- The board replacement swaps only the electronics enclosure outside the water volume. The existing PMT signals are simply digitised better, and the original response can be emulated to keep continuity with archived data.
- It takes under 1 person-hour per station.

## 3. Power and communications reinforcement

**Technology:** an additional or upgraded solar panel, a new battery pair, and a charge-controller update. The radio link firmware is updated to carry the extra data volume.

**Why:** the SSD PMT and faster electronics raise power draw by a few watts. The station must remain autonomous year-round at 100% duty cycle.

## Items considered and excluded or deferred

| Option | Reason |
|---|---|
| Buried muon counters (AMIGA-type scintillators at 2.3 m depth) | Measure muons directly, but excavation exceeds the labour budget and cost across 1,660 stations. Suitable only for a small infill sub-array used for calibration and cross-checks. |
| Radio antennas on stations | Most valuable for inclined showers above 60°, which are outside this goal. Could be a later add-on. |
| Water-volume segmentation or an in-tank small PMT | Forbidden by the no-opening requirement. |
| Fluorescence-site changes (e.g. reduced-gain operation to extend duty cycle) | Useful for cross-calibrating the SSD and electronics mass estimators, but not a station hardware item. |

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a ~3.8 m² plastic-scintillator detector (WLS-fibre, single PMT with dual-gain readout) on the roof of every water-Cherenkov station, read out by upgraded 120 MHz electronics, to separate electromagnetic and muonic signals without touching the sealed tanks.

# Hardware Upgrades for Muon-Number Composition in Showers at 80–84°

## Why inclined showers change the design

At zenith angles of 80–84°, the shower crosses about 6–9 atmospheric depths (roughly 5,500–8,000 g/cm²) of slant atmosphere before reaching the ground. The electromagnetic cascade from shower maximum is almost entirely absorbed. What reaches the stations is:

- mainly muons, which typically make up about 80–90% of the signal; and
- a small electromagnetic "halo" from muon decay and knock-on electrons, which is well modelled and largely corrected for in the standard muon-number analysis.

This has two consequences.

1. **The existing water stations already measure the muon number.** Fitting a muon-density map to the station signals gives the muon content relative to a reference model, the quantity Auger calls N₁₉ or R_μ. In comparable practice this achieves well under 30% resolution at 10^19.5 eV, typically 10–20%. At these angles the shower footprint is tens of km² and elongated, so the 0.7 km grid is dense: each event samples many stations. The tank geometry also suits near-horizontal muons. Each tank has a radius of about 1.9 m and a depth of 1.3 m. Its side profile presents about 2r·h ≈ 4.9 m² to horizontal muons, versus about 11·cos θ ≈ 1.1–1.9 m² from the top. Long, nearly horizontal track lengths give large, clean muon signals.

2. **What is missing is the electromagnetic measurement.** Composition requires the muon number compared with an independent calorimetric energy, or with X_max. Today that energy comes only from fluorescence, about 12% of the time. In inclined events the electromagnetic part of the cascade is gone from the ground, so it must be measured some other way.

## Proposed upgrades

### 1. Radio antenna on every station (primary upgrade)

- **Hardware:** a dual-polarised, wideband antenna (30–80 MHz, SALLA-type or similar), mounted on each tank.
- **Why it fits:** near-horizontal showers produce radio footprints several km across. Many stations on a 0.7 km grid will detect each event above about 10^18.5–10^19 eV.
- **What it measures:** the radiation energy, which gives the electromagnetic energy with roughly 10–15% resolution. This is independent of the fluorescence detectors and available around the clock. Some sensitivity to X_max via the footprint shape is a bonus.
- **Result:** the muon-number-to-electromagnetic-energy ratio, combining tank muons with radio electromagnetic energy, becomes the full-duty-cycle mass estimator. Fluorescence-detector hybrid events serve as cross-calibration.
- **Practical requirements:**
  - low-power digitiser, under a few watts, within the existing solar budget plus a modest panel or battery increase;
  - triggering from the tank, with buffer readout;
  - GPS timing already exists;
  - the radio link must carry small radio-trace payloads for triggered events only.

### 2. Upgraded station electronics

- **Faster, higher-resolution digitisation:** about 120 MHz or more and 12-bit or better. This sharpens the muon "spike" structure and arrival-time profiles, which improves shower-geometry and muon-density fits and residual electromagnetic subtraction.
- **Better timing:** a newer GPS receiver for better than 5 ns relative timing. This improves zenith-angle reconstruction, which matters because the muon-number estimate depends steeply on angle near 80–84°.
- **A shared front end** that also hosts the radio channels, keeping power and communications use efficient.

### 3. Dynamic-range extension (secondary)

- A small photomultiplier tube or low-gain channel to avoid saturation in stations near the core.
- This matters less at these angles, because densities are low and spread out, but it is cheap insurance for the highest-energy events.

### 4. Calibration aids

- Online muon-peak and charge-histogram calibration, retained and improved.
- Tank-level monitoring of water quality and reflectivity, to keep muon-signal systematics at the few-percent level over time.

## What not to prioritise for this programme

- **Scintillator panels on the tank lids:** a flat panel's effective area falls as cos θ, to about 0.1–0.17 at these angles. They would also be measuring an electromagnetic component that has already been absorbed. They are useful for vertical showers, not here.
- **Buried muon counters:** at 80–84° the atmosphere already acts as the absorber, so shielded detectors add cost without a corresponding gain.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a wideband (30–80 MHz) radio antenna with low-power readout on every station, so that the electromagnetic energy of inclined showers is measured full-time and can be paired with the water-tank muon number.

This is an excellent engineering challenge. The key physics goal is to distinguish electromagnetic (e/γ) content from muonic content on an event-by-event basis, since iron primaries produce more muons and fewer electromagnetic particles at ground level than protons at the same energy.

Given the constraints, here are my proposed hardware upgrades:

## 1. **Scintillator Module on Tank Roof (Primary Recommendation)**

Install a ~3 m² plastic scintillator panel (segmented into 2-4 modules of ~1.5 m² each) on top of each water tank, read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs).

**Rationale:**
- The water tank has ~10 radiation lengths of shielding, absorbing most electromagnetic particles while muons penetrate
- The scintillator sees the full shower (EM + muon), while the water sees predominantly muons
- Ratio of scintillator/water signals gives mass-sensitive observable
- Proven concept (AugerPrime is implementing this)

**Technical specs:**
- 3 m² × 3 cm thick extruded scintillator: ~$1,200
- SiPM readout (4-8 channels): ~$800
- Weatherproof enclosure, mounting: ~$600
- Electronics (digitization, integration with existing DAQ): ~$1,200
- Radio telemetry upgrade: ~$400
- Solar panel expansion: ~$600
- Installation hardware/cabling: ~$400
- **Deployment labor per station: ~4 hours**
- **Total: ~$5,200/station**

## 2. **Underground Muon Counter** 

Bury a ~5 m² plastic scintillator panel 2-3 meters below ground adjacent to each station.

**Rationale:**
- Direct measurement of muon content (EM cascade absorbed by overburden)
- Complementary to surface measurements

**Challenges:**
- Excavation time exceeds labor budget (~8-12 hours/station)
- Deployment complexity in rocky terrain
- Cost: ~$4,000-5,000/station (excavation, burial, cabling)

## 3. **Radio Antenna Array for Air-Shower Detection**

Add 30-80 MHz radio antennas (3 orthogonal polarizations) to detect coherent radio emission from shower development.

**Rationale:**
- Radio signal correlates with shower maximum depth (Xmax)
- Low cost per antenna (~$500-800)
- Non-invasive installation

**Challenges:**
- Requires significant additional infrastructure (DAQ, timing, triggering)
- Analysis complexity
- RFI in some locations
- Total cost likely $3,000-4,000/station

## 4. **Externally-Mounted Muon Hodoscope**

Attach segmented scintillator bars to the *sides* of the existing tank (outside the liner, but using the water as shielding).

**Rationale:**
- Horizontal muon counting through water absorber
- Fully external, no tank opening required

**Challenges:**
- Geometrical acceptance is limited
- Calibration complexity
- Cost: ~$4,000-5,000/station

## 5. **Enhanced PMT Timing Electronics**

Upgrade the electronics of the existing 3 PMTs to capture faster time structure of signals.

**Rationale:**
- Muons vs. EM components have different time profiles
- Rise time and pulse shape discrimination

**Challenges:**
- Limited discriminating power
- May not achieve desired mass sensitivity
- Requires intervention in sealed electronics (though not water volume)
- Cost: ~$2,000-3,000/station

---

## Recommended Implementation Strategy

Deploy **roof-mounted scintillator modules** at all 1,660 stations:

- **Month 1-6:** Prototype and test 50 units, refine installation procedures
- **Month 7-18:** Full deployment using teams of 2 (4 person-hours/station)
- Leverage existing GPS timing and radio infrastructure
- Integration with existing trigger and DAQ
- Immediate muon/EM discrimination capability

The scintillator-on-tank approach provides:
- Clean mass-sensitive observable (surface/buried signal ratio)
- Minimal invasiveness (external mounting only)
- Proven physics concept
- Fits budget and labor constraints
- 100% duty cycle operation
- Backward compatibility with existing data

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install 3 m² segmented plastic scintillator panels with SiPM readout on the roof of each water-Cherenkov station to separate electromagnetic and muonic shower components.**

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal for the UHECR Surface Array

## The core problem

The physics goal is event-by-event proton-versus-iron separation above 10^19.5 eV, using the surface array at 100% duty cycle, for zenith angles below 60°.

- **The fluorescence telescopes cannot provide this.** They measure X_max directly, but only about 15% of the time. At the highest energies that leaves only a handful of events per year.
- **The water-Cherenkov tank alone cannot provide it either.** It records one total signal in which electromagnetic (EM) and muonic contributions are mixed.
- **The mass information is in that mixture.** At fixed energy, iron showers have about 40% more muons than proton showers, and they develop earlier (shallower X_max), so less EM signal survives to the ground.
- **The task is to unmix the signal.** This needs a second detector at each station with a different relative response to EM particles and muons. It must also respect the constraints: no opening the tank, no moving it, about $6.2k and 5.8 person-hours per station.

## 1. Surface Scintillator Detector on every tank (primary upgrade)

**Technology**
- A thin, roughly 4 m² plastic-scintillator plane mounted on the tank roof. A practical design is two modules of extruded scintillator bars (about 1 cm thick) read by wavelength-shifting fibres into a single photomultiplier.
- It sits in a light-tight aluminium enclosure with a double roof and sunshade to control temperature.
- It mounts on a support frame bolted to the existing lifting lugs.

**Physics motivation**
- **Different responses.** A thin scintillator responds roughly equally to electrons, photons converting in the roof and muons, counting particles. The 1.2 m water volume is thick, so muons crossing it deposit much more signal than the EM particles, which are mostly absorbed.
- **Signal separation.** Two co-located detectors with different EM/μ response form a 2×2 linear system. Solving it station by station gives separate EM and muon signals at around 1000 m from the core.
- **Mass estimators.** The muon-to-EM ratio, and the muon signal at fixed energy, are mass-sensitive. Combined with the risetime and shower-front curvature already available from the tank, they yield an X_max-like estimator calibrated against fluorescence on the 15% hybrid subset. That calibration then applies to 100% of events.
- **Merit factor.** The expected proton/iron merit factor is about 1.5–2 above 10^19.5 eV. That is enough for statistical mass-enriched samples (for anisotropy studies with a "light" subset) and meaningful event-by-event separation.

**Fit to the constraints**
- **Tank integrity.** The scintillator is an external add-on; tank, liner, water and PMTs are untouched.
- **Weight.** The unit weighs about 150 kg and is lifted by two people or a pickup-mounted davit. The 12 t tank is not moved.
- **Cost.** About $2.5–3k per station including the PMT and high voltage.
- **Deployment.** Pre-assembled modules can be installed by a two-person crew in about 1.5–2 hours on site.
- **Calibration.** The unit self-calibrates using atmospheric muons: the vertical-equivalent MIP peak.

## 2. Upgraded station electronics, mounted outside the water volume

**Technology**
- A new digitiser board in the existing external electronics enclosure, replacing the old board via the existing cable connectors.
- Specifications: about 120 MHz, 12-bit ADCs (versus about 40 MHz, 10-bit); channels for the scintillator PMT plus spares; a modern FPGA/CPU; and an improved GPS receiver with nanosecond-level timing.
- Retained legacy features: the high- and low-gain channels and the old trigger algorithms. These can be run in emulation mode.

**Physics motivation**
- **Common readout.** The tank and scintillator must be read synchronously by the same electronics for the signal unmixing to work.
- **Better timing.** Faster sampling sharpens the muon-dominated early part of the trace, improving risetime and muon-jump estimators, which are additional mass observables. Better timing also improves the shower-front and curvature reconstruction.
- **Continuity with the archive.** The legacy-trigger emulation and an overlap period with a subset of dual-readout stations demonstrate that the tank's response remains identical to the archived data. The detector is unchanged; only its digitisation improves, and that improvement can be cross-checked.

**Cost and deployment:** about $1.5–2k and under 1 person-hour per station (swap the board, update firmware).

## 3. Dynamic-range extension without opening the tank

**Problem**
- Near the core of high-energy events, the tank's PMTs saturate. This loses the stations closest to the core, which carry the most precise lateral-distribution information.

**Rejected option**
- A small PMT inserted into the tank, as some upgrades have done, is excluded here because it requires opening the sealed volume.

**Proposed alternative**
- Provide the scintillator PMT with a dual-gain readout: a dynode and an anode channel, together about 2×10⁴ dynamic range.
- Add a lower-gain readout tap on the existing tank PMT signal in the new electronics.

**Physics motivation:** this recovers near-core stations, giving a better lateral-distribution fit and energy estimate at the highest energies.

**Cost:** essentially included in items 1 and 2.

## 4. Optional, if budget remains: radio antenna on the scintillator frame

**Technology**
- A dual-polarisation 30–80 MHz antenna mounted on the scintillator support frame, read out by the new electronics.

**Physics motivation**
- Radio measures the EM energy calorimetrically. It is most effective for inclined showers (above 60°), which fall outside the stated goal.
- For the target sample it is therefore secondary. It could provide cross-calibration and future extension.

**Cost:** about $1k.

## Rejected for the full array

- **Buried muon counters:** they give a clean muon count, but require excavation of about 10 m² at around 2.3 m depth next to each station. That is far beyond 5.8 person-hours and the budget. They are useful only on a small infill area as a validation of the scintillator–tank unmixing.
- **Any in-tank segmentation, extra PMTs or liner change:** forbidden by the tank-integrity constraint.

## Budget and labour check (per station)

| Item | Cost | Field labour |
|---|---|---|
| Scintillator module, PMT and frame | ~$2.8k | ~2 h |
| Electronics | ~$1.8k | ~0.8 h |
| Cabling, solar power upgrade (extra ~10 W load) and shipping | ~$0.8k | ~1 h |
| Travel overhead | — | ~1.5 h |
| **Total** | **~$5.4k** | **~5.3 h** |

This fits within the $6.2k and 5.8 person-hour envelope, with a margin of about $0.8k per station for the radio antenna or contingency.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Mount a ~4 m² plastic scintillator detector on top of every water-Cherenkov tank, read out synchronously with the tank by new external electronics, to separate the electromagnetic and muonic signals for event-by-event mass estimation.

# Hardware Recommendations for the Teral Plain Array: Composition Phase

## The governing physics

The programme uses showers at 80–84° zenith. At these angles the shower crosses roughly 6–10 vertical atmospheres before reaching the ground. The electromagnetic cascade is almost entirely absorbed long before then. What remains at ground level is overwhelmingly muons, plus a small electromagnetic "halo" from muon decay and knock-on electrons, about 10–20% of the signal.

This has two consequences for the design:

- **The existing water-Cherenkov stations already measure muons.** For these events they are effectively muon counters. Fitting the ground signal to a reference muon-density map gives the muon number directly. Auger's N19 analysis does exactly this, at about 15–20% resolution above 10^19 eV. That already meets the 30% target, so the muon side needs refinement, not a new detector.
- **The electromagnetic component cannot be measured at ground with particle detectors.** It has been absorbed. To measure it separately, you need a detector that sees the cascade in the atmosphere. That points to radio.

The missing piece is an independent, full-time electromagnetic energy estimate. Without it, the muon number cannot be turned into composition. Composition comes from muon number at fixed energy, and the energy scale currently depends on fluorescence data available only 12% of the time.

## Recommendations

### 1. A radio antenna on every station (highest priority)

**What to install:** a dual-polarisation, broadband antenna operating at 30–80 MHz on each of the 1,350 stations. A SALLA (short aperiodic loaded loop antenna) design, as used for the AugerPrime Radio Detector, is a good choice. It is low-gain, so its response is weakly dependent on the ground, and it is robust in wind.

**Supporting electronics:**
- low-noise amplifiers;
- a digitiser of at least 250 MS/s;
- readout triggered by the existing water-Cherenkov trigger, so the radio channel needs no self-trigger.

**Why radio:**
- The radio emission (geomagnetic plus Askaryan) is produced by the electromagnetic cascade in the air. Its integrated energy measures the electromagnetic energy calorimetrically, to about 10–15%.
- The atmosphere is transparent at these frequencies, so the measurement works day and night in all weather: 100% duty cycle.
- At 80–84° the radio footprint spans several to tens of km². A 0.7 km grid therefore samples each event at many stations. Inclined showers are the regime where sparse radio arrays work best.
- Radio and water-Cherenkov together give electromagnetic and muonic measurements for every event. That is exactly the stated requirement.
- The radio footprint also carries some sensitivity to the depth of shower maximum, giving a cross-check against the fluorescence sites.

**Cost and power:** each antenna draws a few watts. The solar budget should be checked, but this is modest.

### 2. Do NOT install surface scintillators

Flat scintillator panels on the tank lids, as in the AugerPrime SSD, are designed to separate electromagnetic from muonic signal at moderate angles, below about 60°. At 80–84° they fail for three reasons:
- their projected area falls as cos θ, to roughly 10–17% of the area seen by a vertical shower;
- there is almost no electromagnetic signal left to measure;
- they would add cost and power while contributing essentially nothing to this programme.

Buried muon counters are also unnecessary here: the atmosphere has already acted as the absorber.

### 3. Upgrade the station electronics

**What to install:** faster, higher-resolution digitisers, of at least 120 MHz and 12 bits or more, on the photomultiplier channels.

**Why:**
- Inclined-shower muons arrive as sharp, flat-front pulses. Finer sampling lets muon-like spikes be separated from the smoother electromagnetic halo, which reduces the halo correction uncertainty in the muon number.
- Better timing improves the arrival-direction and core reconstruction. That matters because the muon-map fit is sensitive to zenith at these steep angles.
- A shared, upgraded electronics board can also host the radio readout.

### 4. Add a small photomultiplier to each station for dynamic range

**What to install:** a small photomultiplier, around 1 inch, with low gain.

**Why:** at 10^19.5 eV, stations near the core saturate. Recovering those signals tightens the muon-density fit and helps hold the resolution well below 30%.

### 5. Improve timing synchronisation

**What to install:** upgraded GNSS receivers, aiming for timing of order 1 ns. A radio beacon transmitter should be added to correct timing station-to-station.

**Why:** radio interferometric reconstruction needs nanosecond relative timing. This step is cheap and is what unlocks the full value of recommendation 1.

### 6. Water-Cherenkov tanks

Keep the existing tanks as they are. The 1.3 m height gives substantial side area to near-horizontal muons, and the 0.7 km spacing is denser than Auger's, which helps muon sampling. Calibrating the tank response against inclined muons is a software and calibration task, not new hardware.

## Summary

| Change | Purpose | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| Radio antennas (SALLA, 30–80 MHz) | Full-time electromagnetic energy; muon-independent energy scale | Essential |
| Faster digitisers (120 MHz or more, 12+ bit) | Muon/halo separation, timing | High |
| Small photomultiplier | Dynamic range near the core | High |
| Nanosecond GNSS plus beacon | Radio reconstruction | Required for radio |
| Surface scintillators | Ineffective at 80–84° | Do not install |

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a dual-polarisation 30–80 MHz radio antenna (SALLA-type) on every station to measure the electromagnetic energy of each inclined shower full-time, while the existing water-Cherenkov tanks measure the muon number.

# Design Review Recommendations for Teral Plain Array Upgrade

## Primary Challenge
The current water Cherenkov detectors cannot distinguish muonic from electromagnetic components in real-time, limiting composition studies to the 12% duty cycle when fluorescence detectors operate. To achieve the science goal, we need full-time muon/EM separation.

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. **Underground Muon Detectors (Scintillator Modules)**
**Technology:** Plastic scintillator panels (e.g., 3 m² per station) buried 2-3 meters beneath existing water tanks, read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs).

**Justification:** 
- Soil overburden absorbs electromagnetic component while muons (minimum ionizing particles) penetrate easily
- 2.5 m depth provides ~5 radiation lengths, attenuating EM by factor >10⁴
- Scintillator + SiPM technology is proven (used by Pierre Auger AugerPrime upgrade, IceCube surface array)
- Can achieve <25% muon number resolution at 10^19.5 eV
- SiPMs are robust, low-power, and operate across temperature ranges
- Cost-effective for large arrays (~$3-5K per station including burial)

### 2. **Segmented Water Cherenkov Detectors**
**Technology:** Retrofit existing tanks with vertical water-tight dividers creating 3-4 separate compartments, each with independent PMT readout (total 6-8 PMTs per station).

**Justification:**
- Muons produce narrow Cherenkov cones; EM showers spread laterally
- Multiple independent measurements per station enable pattern recognition
- Timing differences between compartments distinguish vertical muons from EM spread
- Leverages existing infrastructure with minimal modification
- Successfully demonstrated by Pierre Auger collaboration
- Adds redundancy and improves angular resolution

### 3. **Radio Detection Antennas (30-80 MHz)**
**Technology:** 2-3 crossed dipole antennas per station operating in 30-80 MHz band, digitizing at 200 MS/s.

**Justification:**
- Radio emission strength correlates with EM shower energy (coherent Cherenkov emission in air)
- Independent measurement channel uncorrelated with particle detectors
- Operates 24/7 in all weather conditions
- Recent experiments (LOFAR, Tunka-Rex, AERA) achieve ~20% energy resolution
- Combined with water Cherenkov, enables deconvolution of muon component
- Minimal power consumption (important for solar operation)
- Cost: ~$2-3K per station in components

### 4. **Upgraded PMT System with Waveform Digitization**
**Technology:** Replace existing PMTs with high-QE photomultipliers (e.g., Hamamatsu R12199-02) + 12-bit 250 MS/s FADCs with full waveform capture.

**Justification:**
- Current system likely uses single-channel integration, losing timing information
- Waveform shape differs between muon-dominated (sharp peaks) and EM-dominated (broader) signals
- Rise time analysis provides composition discrimination even in single detector
- Time-over-threshold measurements improve dynamic range (10³-10⁶ particles)
- High-QE PMTs improve low-energy threshold and resolution
- Essential for cross-calibration with other detector types
- Modern electronics enable edge processing for real-time event classification

### 5. **Atmospheric Monitoring Stations**
**Technology:** 5-10 distributed weather stations with:
- LIDAR systems (elastic backscatter, 532 nm)
- All-sky cameras
- Aerosol monitors
- Temperature/humidity profiles

**Justification:**
- Water Cherenkov signal depends on atmospheric attenuation
- Muon number extraction requires accurate shower energy, which requires atmospheric corrections
- Currently rely on fluorescence detectors (12% duty), but need continuous monitoring
- Systematic uncertainties in atmospheric conditions limit composition resolution
- Cost: ~$50K per comprehensive station, networked across array
- Critical for achieving 30% muon number resolution requirement

### 6. **Enhanced Timing System**
**Technology:** Upgrade to dual-frequency GPS/Galileo receivers with <3 ns RMS timing precision, plus optical fiber timing distribution to subset of stations.

**Justification:**
- Muon arrival time distribution differs from EM component
- Improved timing enables better shower geometry reconstruction
- Sub-5 ns timing necessary to exploit waveform shape analysis
- Better angular resolution improves muon lateral distribution fitting
- Fiber backbone between clusters reduces systematic timing drifts
- Minimal power impact with modern GNSS chipsets

## Implementation Priority

**Phase 1 (Years 1-2):** Underground muon detectors + waveform digitization upgrade
- Provides immediate, direct muon measurement capability
- Addresses core science requirement

**Phase 2 (Years 2-3):** Radio antennas + atmospheric monitoring
- Adds independent measurement channel
- Reduces systematics

**Phase 3 (Years 3-4):** Detector segmentation for remaining stations
- Optimizes existing infrastructure
- Extends capabilities developed in earlier phases

## Expected Performance
Combined system should achieve:
- ~20% muon number resolution at 10^19.5 eV (exceeds 30% requirement)
- 100% duty cycle for composition studies
- Event-by-event composition discrimination
- Reduced systematic uncertainties by factor of 2-3

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Add 3 m² buried plastic scintillator panels with SiPM readout beneath each station for direct, unambiguous muon detection with >95% duty cycle**

# Hardware Upgrades for the Teral Plain Array: Separating Muons from Electromagnetic Signal in Every Event

## The constraints that shape the choice

- **Every event needs a muon number.** Fluorescence covers only about 12% of the time, so the separation must come from the full-time surface detector, at every station.
- **The water stations cannot separate components alone.** Each records one mixed signal. Electrons, photons and muons all deposit light in the 1.3 m of water.
- **The tank interior is effectively unavailable.** The vessel is closed and one-piece, filled to within 5 cm of the lid. A layered water detector needs an internal divider and a second photomultiplier volume. That would mean opening or replacing all 1,350 tanks.
- **The showers are near-vertical (0–35°).** Separation methods that work only for inclined showers do not help. Methods that work best near vertical are favoured.

## 1. Thin scintillator detector on every station (primary upgrade)

**Hardware**
- A plastic scintillator plane, roughly 1 cm thick and about 4 m², in a light-tight weatherproof box.
- Mounted on a frame just above the tank lid, with a sunroof against heating.
- Light collected by wavelength-shifting fibres routed to one photomultiplier or a silicon photomultiplier array.
- Read by the same station electronics.

**Physics motivation**
- The two detectors respond differently to the two components:
  - The thin scintillator responds roughly to particle number, so it is dominated by electrons and photons.
  - The 1.3 m water volume is dominated by track length, so muons, which cross the full depth, carry relatively more weight.
- The two independent measurements form a 2×2 system with different coefficients for the muon and electromagnetic parts. Solving it, station by station and in the lateral-distribution fit, gives the muon and electromagnetic signals separately.
- The method works best for showers below about 40°, because the flat scintillator's effective area drops at larger zenith angles. This matches the 0–35° programme.
- The 0.7 km grid gives many stations per event above 10^19 eV. Combined fits can therefore reach a muon-number resolution of about 20–30% at 10^19.5 eV, which meets the requirement.
- The fluorescence sites' direct depth-of-maximum data, during their 12% duty cycle, provide the cross-calibration.

## 2. Upgraded station electronics

**Hardware**
- Faster digitisers of about 120 MHz or more, with higher resolution.
- Extra channels for the scintillator.
- Improved timing receivers for the satellite timing.
- A higher-capacity field processor.

**Physics motivation**
- Fine time traces let the muon peaks be separated from the smooth electromagnetic signal within the water trace. This adds a second, partly independent estimate of muon content.
- Better timing sharpens arrival-direction and shower-front-curvature reconstruction.

## 3. Small photomultiplier in each water tank

**Hardware**
- A small-area photomultiplier with extended dynamic range, inserted through the existing photomultiplier ports.
- This keeps the tank sealed.

**Physics motivation**
- Stations close to the core saturate at 10^19.5 eV and above.
- Unsaturated near-core signals improve the lateral-distribution fit and the muon-number estimate for the most energetic events, where statistics are scarcest.

## 4. Power and communications reinforcement

**Hardware**
- Larger solar panels and batteries.
- Radio links with more bandwidth.

**Physics motivation**
- The added detector and faster sampling increase the power draw and data volume.
- The station must keep its continuous, full-time duty cycle, or the exposure advantage over fluorescence is lost.

## 5. Optional: buried muon counters on a calibration sub-array

**Hardware**
- Segmented scintillators buried about 2.3 m deep next to a subset of stations, with the soil shielding out the electromagnetic component.

**Physics motivation**
- They give a direct, nearly pure muon count.
- This calibrates the scintillator–water separation and checks it against hadronic-model systematics.
- It does not replace the per-station upgrade, because burial at all 1,350 sites is too costly.

## Options not chosen

- **Radio antennas:** they are best for inclined showers and their footprint is small for 0–35° showers, so they do not meet the need.
- **Layered water detectors:** they require modifying the closed, nearly full tanks.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a ~4 m² plastic scintillator detector (wavelength-shifting fibre readout) on top of every water-Cherenkov station, giving two detectors with different muon/electromagnetic responses so the muon number can be extracted for every 0–35° event.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Teral Plain Array Composition Programme

## Core Problem Statement

The fundamental challenge is separating muonic from electromagnetic (EM) components in a water-Cherenkov detector that currently records a single mixed signal. Everything below addresses this in some way.

---

## 1. Underground Muon Detectors (UMDs)

**Technology:** Scintillator panels (plastic scintillator, ~30 mm thick) buried at ~2.3 m depth beneath or adjacent to existing stations, covering ~6 m² per unit, read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) with wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibre readout.

**Why:** The overburden shields EM shower particles (electrons, positrons, gammas attenuate to negligible flux below ~2 m of soil equivalent), leaving muons as the dominant signal. This directly measures N_μ shower-by-shower without dependence on simulations for the EM/muon separation. This is the most direct path to the stated science goal. The Auger SD-1500 UMD upgrade demonstrated this approach works at exactly this scale. SiPMs are preferred over PMTs underground for reliability, lower voltage, and better single-particle resolution. At 10^19.5 eV and zenith angles to 35°, the muon lateral distribution function is well-sampled across ~570 km² if even a subset (~10–15%) of stations carry UMDs, provided they are distributed across the full array footprint rather than clustered.

---

## 2. Segmented / Dual-Layer Water-Cherenkov Detectors

**Technology:** Internal horizontal Tyvek-wrapped optical divider installed at mid-depth (~0.65 m) within upgraded stations, creating upper (EM-sensitive) and lower (muon-enriched) layers, each viewed by its own PMT or SiPM. Alternatively, replace the two existing PMTs with one upward-facing and one downward-facing unit at different depths.

**Why:** Muons are minimum-ionising particles and produce a signal largely independent of depth; EM particles are strongly attenuated with depth. The ratio of lower-to-upper layer signals provides a statistical muon/EM discriminator on a per-station basis within the existing footprint, with no excavation required. This complements UMDs: the segmented WCD works at all stations and all times; UMDs give the cleaner absolute calibration. The technique is proven in the HAWC and Auger engineering work. It does not achieve the cleanliness of physical shielding but delivers a usable EM/muon ratio at 30% resolution when combined with the full lateral distribution fit.

---

## 3. Surface Scintillator Detectors (SSDs) Co-located at Every Station

**Technology:** Two 3 m² plastic scintillator units per station, each read by a SiPM via WLS fibre, mounted on the exterior roof of the existing polyethylene vessel, weather-protected by a thin aluminium or fibreglass skin.

**Why:** Scintillators have a much shorter radiation length response relative to WCDs; their signal is dominated by the EM component (electrons, photons) because the large geometric acceptance of the WCD for inclined muon tracks is absent in the thin scintillator. The ratio SSD_signal / WCD_signal provides an EM-sensitive observable that, combined with the WCD total signal, allows the muon signal to be extracted algebraically station by station. This is exactly the AugerPrime SSD strategy and has been demonstrated to recover muon number at the required resolution. SSDs are surface-mounted, requiring no civil engineering, and can be deployed rapidly across the full 1,350-station array.

---

## 4. PMT Upgrade / Addition of a High-Quantum-Efficiency Large-Area PMT or SiPM Array

**Technology:** Replace or supplement the two existing PMTs with a third, smaller (3-inch) PMT with a UV-transparent window (or a 4×4 SiPM tile at ~6×6 mm² per cell), dedicated to the high-signal muon peak, to extend the dynamic range from ~10³ to ~10⁵ photoelectrons per station.

**Why:** At 10^19.5 eV, stations close to the shower core receive very high particle densities and saturate the existing two-PMT readout. Saturation destroys the core-region signal where EM/muon separation is most diagnostic. A small-area high-dynamic-range channel (or an attenuated channel with a neutral density filter on one PMT) restores linearity. This is a low-cost, high-impact electronics and photosensor change. Without it, the composition analysis is biased for the highest-energy and closest-core events, precisely those with the best signal-to-noise.

---

## 5. Upgraded Front-End Electronics and Timing

**Technology:** Replace existing ASICs/ADCs with 120 MHz (or faster) FADC boards (12-bit, dual-gain) per station, with GPS disciplined to <10 ns absolute timing (replace current satellite timing if it exceeds this). Add a low-power FPGA for on-board pulse-shape discrimination.

**Why:** Muons arriving at a station produce a sharper, narrower pulse than the more extended EM component because muon lateral scattering is smaller and their arrival time spread within a shower front is narrower. Pulse-shape analysis (rise time, tail, peak-to-charge ratio) provides an additional muon/EM discriminant on a per-station basis, independent of hardware segmentation. 120 MHz FADCs resolve pulses of ~8 ns, sufficient to separate muon peaks from EM halos in the time trace. This upgrade also improves shower front timing for better angular resolution (currently limiting composition at large zenith angles).

---

## 6. Additional Fluorescence Detector Stations or Enhanced Duty-Cycle Telescope Technology

**Technology:** Two or three additional fluorescence telescope sites at the array perimeter (3 × 6 telescopes, 30° elevation × 60° azimuth FoV, using new-generation 20 cm SiPM-based cameras replacing PMT cameras), plus an infra-red cloud monitor and improved aerosol LIDAR at each site.

**Why:** The existing 12% duty cycle of the fluorescence detectors is the limiting factor for absolute energy scale and X_max cross-calibration. The mass composition programme ultimately ties array muon observables to X_max measurements; a larger FD exposure directly reduces the systematic uncertainty in this calibration. SiPM cameras tolerate higher night-sky background and can operate in partially moonlit conditions, potentially raising effective duty cycle to 18–22%. Additional sites improve X_max resolution by reducing average distance to shower maximum. LIDAR and cloud monitoring reduce systematic energy-scale uncertainty from atmospheric variation, which otherwise propagates directly into the muon-number normalisation.

---

## 7. Radio Detection Antennas

**Technology:** Butterfly or AERA-style logarithmic periodic dipole antennas (30–80 MHz band) mounted on a ~300 m sub-grid (every third station), read out by a 200 MHz FADC, synchronised to the existing station GPS timing.

**Why:** Radio emission from air showers is dominated by geomagnetic and charge-excess mechanisms in the EM cascade. The radio signal amplitude and lateral distribution measure the EM energy of the shower independently of the WCD, providing a clean EM component estimator that is free of the muon contamination that complicates WCD EM reconstruction. EM energy from radio + muon number from UMDs/SSDs gives a two-observable composition analysis that breaks the degeneracy between energy and mass. Radio operates 100% of the time (full-time exposure, meeting the stated requirement), is unaffected by clouds, and adds no dead time to the array. The technique is now sufficiently mature (from Tunka-Rex, AERA, LOFAR) that it is a credible proposal item.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Role |
|---|---|---|
| Underground Muon Detector | Buried plastic scintillator + SiPM | Direct N_μ measurement |
| Segmented WCD | Internal optical divider + extra PMT | Per-station EM/μ ratio |
| Surface Scintillator Detector | Thin plastic scintillator + SiPM + WLS | EM component isolation |
| High-dynamic-range photosensor | Small PMT / SiPM tile + attenuated channel | Saturation recovery near core |
| Fast FADC + pulse-shape FPGA | 120 MHz 12-bit dual-gain FADC | Pulse-shape μ/EM discrimination |
| Extended FD + SiPM cameras | SiPM FD cameras + LIDAR + cloud monitor | X_max calibration, energy scale |
| Radio antennas | 30–80 MHz LDPA on sub-grid | Independent EM energy, 100% duty cycle |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Underground muon detectors (buried plastic scintillator with SiPM readout beneath a representative sub-array of stations), because they provide a direct, physically clean measurement of the muon component through EM shielding rather than statistical decomposition, making them the most robust single path to achieving the required 30% muon-number resolution across the full array exposure.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Pierre Auger Surface Detector Array

## Core Physics Problem

The fundamental challenge is separating the muonic signal (mass-sensitive) from the electromagnetic (EM) signal within each station's single integrated measurement. Iron-induced showers produce ~60–80% more muons than proton showers at the same energy. Without muon/EM separation, the mass estimator relies on shower universality arguments with large systematic uncertainties. The goal requires event-by-event sensitivity, not just statistical separation.

---

## Upgrade Concept Hierarchy

### **1. Surface Scintillator Overlay — PRIMARY RECOMMENDATION**

**Physics rationale:** A plastic scintillator panel placed *on top of* each water-Cherenkov station (WCD) measures the EM + muon particle density at ground level, but with a different EM/muon weighting than the WCD beneath it. The WCD signal is dominated by the muon contribution at large core distances (muons are minimum-ionizing and traverse the full 1.2 m; EM particles are largely absorbed). The scintillator, being thin (~1 cm), is relatively *more* sensitive to EM particles per particle than the deep WCD. The ratio of the two signals provides, station-by-station, an estimator of the local muon fraction, hence primary mass.

This is precisely the AugerPrime upgrade that was actually designed and deployed — validating the approach.

**Hardware specification:**

| Item | Specification |
|------|--------------|
| Scintillator tile | 3.8 m² × 1 cm thick extruded polystyrene scintillator (e.g., Fermilab/NOvA-type tiles or equivalent), two panels of ~1.9 m² each |
| Wavelength-shifting fibre | 1 mm double-clad Y-11 WLS fibre routed in grooves, ~200 m per station total |
| Photosensor | 1 × SiPM (silicon photomultiplier, e.g., Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE or equivalent), 6×6 mm², one per panel |
| Light-tight enclosure | Aluminium extrusion housing with Tyvek inner lining, UV-stabilised polyurethane outer coat |
| Mechanical mounting | Aluminium frame bolted to existing tank flange bolts (no penetration of tank); four M12 stainless studs |
| Electronics | Small-signal amplifier + discriminator board, 12-bit ADC at 120 MHz, FPGA timestamping, integrated with new unified board (see item 3) |
| Weight on tank lid | ~25 kg, well within lid load rating |

**Signal separation principle:**

Define $S_\text{WCD}$ (VEM units) and $S_\text{SSD}$ (MIP units). Then:

$$\frac{S_\text{WCD}}{S_\text{SSD}} \propto \frac{a \cdot N_\mu \cdot \langle S_\mu^\text{WCD}\rangle + N_\text{EM} \cdot \langle S_\text{EM}^\text{WCD}\rangle}{b \cdot N_\mu \cdot \langle S_\mu^\text{SSD}\rangle + N_\text{EM} \cdot \langle S_\text{EM}^\text{SSD}\rangle}$$

Since $\langle S_\mu^\text{WCD}\rangle / \langle S_\text{EM}^\text{WCD}\rangle \gg \langle S_\mu^\text{SSD}\rangle / \langle S_\text{EM}^\text{SSD}\rangle$ (by roughly a factor 3–4 for 1.2 m water depth vs. 1 cm scintillator), the ratio is a strong muon-fraction estimator, with ~20–25% muon number resolution per station at relevant distances, translating to ln A resolution of ~0.5 on an event-by-event basis above 10^19.5 eV where shower sizes are large.

| Solar panel upgrade (12 W additional, see item 4) | 480 |
| GPS/comms (shared, no extra cost) | 0 |
| Cabling, connectors, misc | 220 |
| Deployment labour materials | 390 |
| **Subtotal hardware** | **~4,900** |
| Contingency + logistics | ~900 |
| **Total per station** | **~5,800** |

This is within the $6,200 budget, leaving ~$400 margin.

### **2. Underground Muon Detector (Buried Scintillator) — CONSIDERED BUT DEPRIORITIZED**

**Physics:** Burying a ~10 m² scintillator panel 2.3 m underground beside each station achieves nearly pure muon counting (EM shielded by ~540 g/cm² of soil). This is the approach used by the AMIGA muon counter at Auger.
