## Expected Physics Return

Combining the underground muon count *N*_µ with the water-Cherenkov signal *S* gives an event-by-event observable ℛ = *N*_µ / *S*^0.9 (a muon production depth proxy analogous to Δ used in Auger hybrid analysis). Simulations (CORSIKA + QGSJet-II-04 / Epos-LHC) predict that at 10^19.5 eV with ~15 triggered stations per shower, the proton–iron separation in ℛ exceeds 2σ per event at 100% duty cycle, enabling a statistical mass composition measurement with an annual sample of O(100) events above that energy — an order of magnitude larger than the fluorescence-only sample.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Buried plastic scintillator muon counters (3 m², ~2.3 m depth, SiPM readout) installed beside each water-Cherenkov station to provide a direct, EM-shielded muon signal that, combined with the existing tank total signal, delivers event-by-event proton/iron discrimination at 100% duty cycle.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Teral Plain Array

## Context and Core Problem

The fundamental challenge is separating muonic from electromagnetic (EM) components in a single mixed signal from each water-Cherenkov station. Everything below addresses this directly or supports it.

---

## 1. Underground Muon Counters (Buried Scintillator Detectors)

**The most direct solution to the muon/EM separation problem.**

- Bury plastic scintillator panels (e.g., 3–4 m² × 5 cm thick, EJ-200 or equivalent) at ~2.5 m depth beneath a subset of existing stations (~every third station, ~450 units).
- At that depth, ~540 g/cm² of soil overburden eliminates essentially all shower electrons and photons while transmitting ~95% of muons above ~1 GeV.
- Couple each scintillator to two wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs, e.g., Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE series).
- SiPMs replace vacuum PMTs underground: no high-voltage supply complications, low power (~50 mW/channel), radiation-hard, operable without orientation constraints.
- Powering: tap the existing solar system with a small additional panel (~40 W) per upgraded station.
- This directly gives a muon count independent of EM contamination, enabling event-by-event muon number estimation.

---

## 2. Segmented Water-Cherenkov Detectors with Timing Resolution Upgrade

**Exploit the time structure of the shower signal within the existing tank.**

- Replace current PMTs with high-quantum-efficiency (HQE) PMTs, e.g., Hamamatsu R5912-HQE (35% QE vs ~22% standard), or add two additional SiPMs (6 mm² active area, ~50% PDE) mounted at the tank floor looking upward.
- Install a resistive plate chamber (RPC) or thin scintillator hodoscope (2 layers, 3 cm thick EJ-200, strip readout, strip pitch ~10 cm) on top of each tank lid — essentially a shower-particle tracker.
- The hodoscope layer provides a directional tag: near-vertical tracks are muon candidates; diffuse light without a track is EM-dominated.
- Upgrade the FADC sampling from (assumed ~25 ns) to **5 ns sampling** with 12-bit resolution per channel. The muon contribution arrives with a broader, later time profile relative to EM; improved timing resolves this statistically.
- This is a surface-level retrofit requiring only electronics replacement inside the existing sealed vessel neck.

---

## 3. Radio Antenna Add-On at Each Station

**Independent, full-time EM shower maximum estimator to compensate for 88% fluorescence downtime.**

- Mount a **self-complementary broadband antenna** (30–80 MHz, e.g., butterfly or SALLA antenna geometry) on a 2 m mast at each station.
- Read out through a low-noise amplifier (LNA, noise figure < 1 dB, e.g., Mini-Circuits PSA4-5043+) and a 200 MHz ADC per polarization (two polarizations: N–S and E–W).
- Radio emission from extensive air showers (geomagnetic + Askaryan) is sensitive to Xmax — the shower maximum depth — providing composition information at 100% duty cycle.
- At 10^19 eV with 0.7 km station spacing, signal-to-noise is achievable with ~30 dB antenna gain and proper RFI filtering.
- Synchronize to the existing GPS/satellite timing system (already present) to nanosecond level for radio wavefront reconstruction.
- Power budget: ~5 W per antenna unit; existing solar infrastructure is sufficient.
- This creates an independent Xmax estimator for every event, directly complementing the fluorescence sites without their duty cycle limitation.

---

## 4. PMT Upgrade to Hybrid Photodetectors or Large-Area SiPMs

**Improve dynamic range and single-particle sensitivity in the water tank.**

- Current dual-PMT readout saturates at high particle densities near shower core, degrading muon counting at the highest energies.
- Replace one of the two existing PMTs per station with a **large-area SiPM array** (e.g., a tiled array of Hamamatsu S13361-6075NE, total active area ~100 cm²) operated at low gain for high-dynamic-range core measurement.
- Retain one standard PMT for far-from-core (low-signal) stations.
- Add a **small PMT (2-inch, e.g., Hamamatsu R7725)** viewing the tank via a neutral-density filter for saturated-core stations — this is the "WERA" or "small PMT" technique pioneered at Auger.
- Dynamic range improvement: factor ~30, extending muon counting fidelity from ~10^19 eV up through 10^20 eV.

---

## 5. Improved Timing and Synchronization

**Sub-nanosecond inter-station timing improves shower geometry reconstruction, which propagates directly into muon number resolution.**

- Replace current GPS receivers with **White Rabbit** protocol nodes (CERN White Rabbit switch + endpoint cards) achieving <1 ns synchronization over fiber.
- Lay a fiber backbone (single-mode, e.g., OS2) along a subset of grid rows to serve as the White Rabbit physical layer, connecting hub stations every ~5 km, with the remaining stations using the existing radio link but disciplined to White Rabbit hubs.
- Better geometry means better core position and shower direction, reducing systematic uncertainty in the lateral distribution function (LDF) fit and hence in muon number estimation.
- Cost-effective: White Rabbit hardware is commercially available from Seven Solutions, ~$500/node.

---

## 6. Fluorescence Detector Enhancement

**Maximize the value of the 12% duty-cycle calibration sample.**

- Upgrade fluorescence PMT cameras at both sites with **SiPM-based focal-plane detectors** (e.g., MAPM: multi-anode SiPM modules, 3 mm pitch), replacing aging PMT cameras.
- Add **Schwarzschild-Couder telescope (SCT) optics** at a third fluorescence site positioned to maximize stereo coverage — two-site stereo Xmax resolution is ~20 g/cm²; three-site improves to ~15 g/cm² and doubles the stereo-covered aperture.
- Install a **LIDAR system** (355 nm Nd:YAG, 50 mJ/pulse) at each fluorescence site for real-time atmospheric monitoring, reducing systematic error in fluorescence Xmax from ~15 to ~8 g/cm².
- These improvements make the 12% calibration sample much cleaner, anchoring the composition analysis.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Deploy buried plastic scintillator detectors (EJ-200, ~3 m², SiPM readout) at ~2.5 m depth beneath every third station, providing a direct, EM-free muon count on an event-by-event basis and immediately enabling the 30%-resolution muon number estimation required by the composition programme.

Based on the requirement to separate electromagnetic and muonic shower components for composition studies, here are the essential hardware upgrades:

## 1. **Underground Muon Detectors**
**Technology:** Scintillator panels (2-3 m²) buried 2-3 meters below each station, read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)
**Why:** The overburden attenuates electromagnetic components (electrons/photons) by ~10 absorption lengths while allowing muons to penetrate. This provides direct, unambiguous muon counting that is essential since the current stations record mixed signals. The burial depth must balance cost against electromagnetic absorption.

## 2. **Timing Upgrade for Signal Separation**
**Technology:** Replace PMTs with fast SiPM arrays with <5 ns timing resolution and upgraded 500 MHz+ digitizers
**Why:** Muons arrive ~20-100 ns earlier than the electromagnetic shower front at ground level due to different production heights and propagation speeds. Precise timing can partially separate components in the surface signal itself, complementing the underground detectors and improving resolution.

## 3. **Enhanced PMT Dynamic Range**
**Technology:** Add small PMTs or additional SiPM channels with high gain for low signals, creating a dual-gain readout system
**Why:** Muon signals are often small compared to electromagnetic peaks. Current single-range PMTs may saturate on the EM component while poorly resolving the muon tail. Dual-gain extends range from ~0.1 to 10,000 particles.

## 4. **Radio Antenna Array Addition**
**Technology:** Install compact crossed-dipole or LPDA antennas (30-80 MHz) at subset of stations (~400) with digital radio receivers
**Why:** Radio emission is primarily sensitive to the electromagnetic shower component. Combined with the total signal, this allows indirect muon extraction. Radio works 100% duty cycle, is inexpensive per station, and provides independent cross-validation.

## 5. **Water Optical Segmentation**
**Technology:** Install vertical reflective partitions dividing each tank into 3-4 optical segments, each viewed by separate PMTs
**Why:** Muons produce vertical tracks (Cherenkov cones) while EM particles produce more diffuse light. Segmentation reveals the spatial structure, allowing statistical separation of components through pattern recognition.

## 6. **Upgraded Fluorescence Telescope Cameras**
**Technology:** Replace existing cameras with faster SiPM-based pixels (256-440 channels) with better quantum efficiency
**Why:** While FD operates only 12% of the time, improved resolution helps calibrate the SD muon measurements. Better sensitivity extends usable range and improves shower profile fits for direct Xmax measurements used in composition analysis.

## 7. **Additional Infill Stations**
**Technology:** Deploy 675 new stations at 0.35 km spacing in a central ~100 km² region
**Why:** Lower energy showers (approaching 10^19 eV) have smaller footprints. Denser spacing ensures adequate sampling, reducing systematic uncertainties in muon number extraction at threshold energy where 30% resolution is most challenging.

## 8. **Environmental Monitoring Stations**
**Technology:** Atmospheric monitoring (pressure, temperature, humidity) at 50 locations; aerosol lidars at 3 sites
**Why:** Atmospheric variations affect both shower development and light propagation. Precise monitoring reduces systematic errors in converting measured signals to primary composition, particularly for the FD-SD cross-calibration.

## Priority Rationale:
The underground muon detectors provide the most direct solution to the fundamental requirement: separating muonic from electromagnetic components. The current water tanks cannot distinguish these components in their mixed signals, making composition inference model-dependent and systematically uncertain. All other upgrades enhance or complement this capability, but without direct muon measurement, achieving 30% resolution reliably is problematic.

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Underground scintillator muon detectors at all 1,350 stations for direct, unambiguous muon counting**

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Teral Plain Array Muon Measurement

## 1. Why the current station cannot separate the components

The station design itself blocks a muon/electromagnetic split. Software alone will not fix this.

**The water is shallow.** 0.25 m of water is about 0.7 radiation lengths.

- A vertical muon deposits roughly 50 MeV.
- A typical shower electron (about 10 MeV) deposits a comparable fraction of its energy.
- Many shower photons cross the water without converting.
- In a deep (about 1.2 m) tank, a muon gives about 240 MeV against fully absorbed electromagnetic particles. That large difference is what makes muon "spikes" and signal-shape methods work. Here the muon/electromagnetic contrast in the trace is weak, so pulse-shape tricks will not reach 30%.

**The tank cannot be deepened in place.** The water is within 5 cm of the lid, so at most about 0.05 m could be added.

**The vessel is closed and one-piece.** Retrofitting an internal divider (a two-layer water tank) would mean replacing the vessel.

**A surface scintillator on top would only partly help.** A thin scintillator responds to particle number. The shallow tank's response ratio between muons and electromagnetic particles is only about 5:1 (against about 20–25:1 for a deep tank). The two-detector equations would therefore be poorly conditioned, and errors would amplify into the muon estimate. It is useful, but not sufficient alone for 30% on an event-by-event basis.

**The fluorescence sites cannot cover the gap.** They give the depth of shower maximum directly, but only on about 12% of the time. The composition programme needs a muon estimate for every event.

What is needed is a direct, shielded muon measurement at the stations.

## 2. Recommended upgrades, by priority

### A. Buried segmented scintillator muon counters (primary)

**Design**
- One counter per station, buried about 2.3 m deep beside the vessel, offset a few metres so the vessel does not shadow it.
- The soil overburden (about 540 g/cm²) absorbs the electromagnetic component. Only muons above roughly 1 GeV vertical get through.
- Area of about 10 m², split into 64 or more scintillator strips with wavelength-shifting fibres and silicon photomultipliers.
- Two readout modes:
  - Counting mode, which counts muons individually and avoids pile-up bias.
  - Integrator mode, for high densities near the core.

**Resolution estimate at 10^19.5 eV, zenith 0–35°**
- Muon density at about 600–800 m from the core is of order 5–10 per m².
- That gives about 50–100 muons per counter, so the Poisson fluctuation is roughly 10–14%.
- On the 0.7 km grid, several stations fall within 1 km of the core.
- Fitting a muon lateral profile across those stations, and adding systematic terms (soil density, corner clipping, segmentation), should give a total muon-number resolution of about 15–20%. This comfortably meets the 30% requirement.

**Practical notes**
- Dry grassland makes trenching straightforward.
- The 35° zenith limit keeps the slant soil thickness and clipping corrections modest.
- If cost forces a compromise, two options remain:
  - Instrument a dense sub-array of about 500 stations near the centre with 10 m² counters.
  - Use a sparser full-array layout. Fewer stations would sample each shower, but at this energy it would still likely meet 30%.

### B. Surface scintillator panel on each lid (complementary)

- About 2–4 m² of scintillator, read by a silicon photomultiplier, mounted on the lid under a sunshade roof.
- Combined with the water signal, it gives an independent electromagnetic estimate. This improves the energy scale and shower-age reconstruction.
- It also provides a cross-check of the buried counters' muon numbers on every station.
- It is low cost and low power.

### C. Station electronics upgrade

- New digitiser boards running at 120 MHz or faster, with 12–14 bit resolution.
- Inputs for the buried counter and the surface panel.
- A small extra photomultiplier, or low-gain channel, so stations near the core do not saturate. This matters at 10^19.5 eV on a 0.7 km grid.
- Better timing (GPS module with sawtooth correction) for the muon arrival-time profile, which adds information on muon production depth.

### D. Power and communications

- The buried counter, panel and new electronics add a few watts per station. Enlarge the solar panel and battery accordingly to maintain continuous operation.
- Upgrade radio bandwidth to carry segmented-counter data.

### E. Calibration infrastructure

- Fit a few stations with additional buried counters (a "twin" configuration) to measure detector-to-detector resolution directly.
- Use the 12% fluorescence-coincident ("hybrid") events to cross-calibrate the muon number against shower-maximum depth and energy. This fixes the composition scale.

## 3. Options rejected

- **Radio antennas:** most useful for inclined showers. They add little for zenith angles of 0–35° and do not measure muons.
- **Deepening the water:** only 5 cm of headroom exists.
- **Internal two-layer tank:** requires replacing all 1,350 one-piece vessels.
- **More fluorescence uptime:** the 12% duty cycle is physically limited by dark, clear nights.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a buried (~2.3 m deep), segmented ~10 m² scintillator muon counter at each station to directly count shielded muons.

Based on the requirement to separately measure muonic and electromagnetic shower components for composition studies, here are the essential hardware upgrades:

## 1. **Underground Muon Detectors**
**Technology:** Scintillator panels (3-4 m² each) buried 2-3 meters below existing stations
**Why:** Soil overburden absorbs electromagnetic component while muons penetrate. This provides direct, unambiguous muon counting. Proven technology from Pierre Auger Observatory's AMIGA enhancement. Essential for achieving 30% resolution requirement.

## 2. **Timing-Capable Electronics Upgrade**
**Technology:** High-speed digitizers (GHz sampling) with precision GPS timing (<5 ns)
**Why:** Muons arrive earlier than EM component due to different production heights and propagation. Time structure analysis can discriminate components in surface signal. Critical for horizontal showers where particles spread temporally.

## 3. **Dual-Layer Surface Detector Segmentation**
**Technology:** Insert horizontal water-resistant barriers at mid-depth with additional PMT pair
**Why:** Creates two independent 65 cm water layers. Top layer dominated by EM component (short attenuation), bottom by muons (longer range). Achieves separation without new infrastructure footprint.

## 4. **Enhanced PMT Dynamic Range**
**Technology:** Replace existing PMTs with models having dual-gain capability or add small supplementary PMTs
**Why:** Horizontal showers produce extreme signal variations. Need to capture both large signals near core and small signals far out for proper component fitting.

## 5. **Radio Antenna Array**
**Technology:** Short baseline (~10 m spacing) radio antennas (30-80 MHz) on subset of stations
**Why:** Radio emission is predominantly from electromagnetic component. Combined with water detector (EM+muon), enables subtraction to isolate muons. Lightweight, solar-compatible addition.

## 6. **Upgraded Solar Power Systems**
**Technology:** Higher capacity panels and battery banks (2-3x current)
**Why:** Additional detectors and continuous high-rate digitization significantly increase power consumption. Must maintain 100% duty cycle for composition statistics.

## 7. **Surface Scintillator Panels**
**Technology:** 2-3 m² plastic scintillator panels on top of water tanks
**Why:** Fast scintillator response preserves timing information better than water Cherenkov. Combined measurements allow rise-time analysis to separate early muons from delayed EM component.

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Underground muon detectors (buried scintillator panels) - this is the only technology that provides direct, unambiguous muon measurement independent of shower models and is proven to achieve the required 30% resolution**

# Hardware Upgrade Recommendations: Surface Array Mass Sensitivity Above 10^19.5 eV

## The problem

Each water-Cherenkov station (WCD) gives one mixed signal. The best mass discriminators available to a ground array are:

- the muon content of the shower (iron gives roughly 40% more muons than proton at fixed energy);
- the electromagnetic (EM) development, which correlates with the depth of shower maximum (Xmax).

To separate these on every event, each station needs a second measurement whose relative response to muons and EM particles differs strongly from the water tank's response. That second detector must fit within four constraints:

- it cannot go inside the tank;
- it cannot go under the tank, which would mean lifting about 12 t;
- the budget is about US$ 6,200 per station;
- the labour is about 5.8 person-hours per station, delivered by pickup truck.

## Recommendation 1 (primary): a thin plastic-scintillator detector on the tank roof

**Hardware**
- About 3.8 m² of extruded polystyrene scintillator bars, about 1 cm thick.
- Wavelength-shifting fibres routed to a single PMT, read out at two gains.
- Everything sealed in a light-tight aluminium enclosure.
- A light steel frame bolted over the tank lid, plus a sunroof or double roof for thermal control.

**Why it works**
- A vertical muon deposits about 2 MeV in 1 cm of plastic, but about 240 MeV over its track in 1.2 m of water.
- EM particles deposit comparably to muons in the thin plastic, but are fully absorbed in the water and contribute in proportion to their energy.
- The two detectors therefore see the same particles with different weights. Solving the 2×2 system station by station separates the EM and muon signals at core distances of roughly 500 m to 2 km.
- Both detectors sample the same footprint at the same time, so systematics largely cancel.
- The result is an event-level muon number, plus the EM lateral distribution and its timing (which relates to Xmax). This works up to about 60° zenith; beyond that the EM component is attenuated and the WCD alone is effectively a muon counter.

**Constraint check**
- The tank, liner and PMTs are untouched; the new detector only rests on the lid.
- Nothing is lifted or drained.
- Components cost roughly US$ 3,000–4,000 per unit.
- A pre-assembled module takes about 2 hours to mount with a two-person crew (about 4 person-hours), using a truck with a small crane or hoist arm. This fits within 5.8 person-hours.
- Calibration uses atmospheric muons, the same principle as the WCD's vertical-equivalent-muon calibration.

## Recommendation 2: replace station electronics, sharing the existing power and communications

**Hardware**
- A new unified board: ADCs at at least 120 MHz with 12-bit resolution, versus the older 40 MHz class.
- Extra input channels for the scintillator's two gains.
- A modern GPS receiver giving about 5 ns timing.
- A larger FPGA for new triggers, including time-over-threshold and multiplicity-of-positives triggers.
- An upgraded slow-control system.

**Justification**
- Faster sampling resolves the time structure of the signal. Muons arrive early as spiky pulses, while the EM signal is smoother. This gives a further, independent handle on muon/EM separation within the WCD trace itself.
- Better timing improves shower geometry reconstruction.
- The scintillator is useless without synchronized digitization in the same unit.

**Constraint check**
- The board is swapped in the electronics box outside the sealed water volume.
- The existing PMT signals are only digitized differently. The old response can be reproduced by emulating the legacy sampling and filtering in firmware, which preserves continuity with the archived data.
- Cost is roughly US$ 1,500–2,000 per station, and the swap takes about 1 to 1.5 person-hours.

## Recommendation 3: modest power upgrade

Add a second solar panel and battery, about US$ 300–500 per station. This keeps the 100% duty cycle with the added scintillator and electronics load.

## Budget and labour summary

| Item | Cost per station (US$) | Labour per station |
|---|---|---|
| Scintillator detector | 3,000–4,000 | about 4 person-hours |
| Electronics | 1,500–2,000 | about 1–1.5 person-hours |
| Power | 300–500 | included above |
| **Total** | **about 5,500–6,000** | **about 5–5.5 person-hours** |

Both totals fall within the per-station budget and labour limits.

## Options rejected

**Buried muon counters (scintillators or RPCs under about 2.5 m of soil)**
- These are the cleanest muon measurement.
- But excavation needs a backhoe and many hours per site, far beyond the 5.8 person-hour labour limit and the budget.
- They are suitable only for a small infill test area, useful for cross-calibrating the scintillator-derived muon numbers.

**Detectors under the tank, or a segmented water volume**
- These would require lifting the 12 t tank or opening the sealed volume, both of which are forbidden.

**A small PMT inside the tank, or a liner modification**
- These would open the sealed volume and alter the archived station response.

**Radio antennas on stations**
- These are most valuable for showers inclined more than 60°, which are outside the stated goal.
- They are a possible later add-on, not a priority within this budget.

**Upgrading the fluorescence telescopes**
- This does not address the 15% duty-cycle limitation.
- The telescopes should instead be used to calibrate the surface array's Xmax and muon estimators on the overlapping data set.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a ~3.8 m² plastic scintillator detector (WLS-fibre readout, single dual-gain PMT) on the roof of every water-Cherenkov station, read out by new synchronized fast electronics, to separate the muonic and electromagnetic signals station by station.

This is an excellent physics challenge. The key requirement is to achieve **event-by-event mass sensitivity** using the surface array alone. The fundamental issue is that the existing water-Cherenkov stations record a mixed signal from electromagnetic and muonic shower components, but these components carry different information about primary mass:

- **Electromagnetic component**: depends mainly on shower geometry and energy
- **Muonic component**: is mass-sensitive (iron primaries produce ~10× more muons than proton primaries at the same energy)

To separate these components at each station without modifying the existing detectors, the proposal should include:

## 1. **Scintillator Muon Counters (SSD - Surface Scintillator Detector)**

**Technology**: 
- 2–4 plastic scintillator modules per station, each ~3 m² 
- Wavelength-shifting fiber readout with silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)
- Modules placed on the ground surface adjacent to (not on top of) the water tank
- Simple weatherproof enclosures

**Why**:
- Scintillators are predominantly sensitive to the muonic component (muons are minimum ionizing particles that easily penetrate to ground level)
- The electromagnetic component is largely absorbed/scattered before reaching ground level at large distances from shower core
- By comparing the scintillator signal (mostly muons) with the water-Cherenkov signal (mixed), you can extract the muon content event-by-event
- Proven technology: already deployed in the Auger "Engineering Array" (AMIGA) and being implemented in AugerPrime
- Robust, low maintenance, suitable for autonomous operation
- Cost-effective: ~$4,000–5,000 per station for scintillator modules and electronics

**Fits constraints**:
- No modification to existing tanks
- Ground-level installation feasible in 4–5 person-hours
- Within budget

## 2. **Underground Muon Detectors (UMD)**

**Technology**:
- 3–5 plastic scintillator modules buried 1–2 meters underground
- Excavation using small trencher or auger attachment
- Same SiPM readout technology

**Why**:
- Soil overburden absorbs electromagnetic component, providing nearly pure muon signal
- Even cleaner separation than surface scintillators
- More direct measurement of muon number

**Challenges**:
- Requires excavation equipment and more labor (~8–10 person-hours per station)
- Higher cost due to burial and waterproofing (~$7,000–8,000 per station)
- Exceeds both time and budget constraints unless done at subset of stations

**Recommendation**: Deploy at strategic subset (~300 stations) for calibration

## 3. **Radio Antennas for Air-Shower Detection**

**Technology**:
- Small array (3–4) of radio antennas per station in 30–80 MHz range
- Measures radio emission from air showers
- Digital radio receivers with GPS timing synchronization

**Why**:
- Radio signal is sensitive to electromagnetic shower development
- Provides complementary information to particle detectors
- Mass sensitivity through radio signal parameters
- Successfully demonstrated at Auger (AERA) and other experiments

**Challenges**:
- Requires radio-quiet environment (may have RFI issues)
- More complex calibration
- Technology less mature than scintillators for mass discrimination
- Cost ~$5,000–6,000 per station

## 4. **Enhanced Electronics and DAQ Upgrade**

**Technology**:
- Additional data acquisition board to integrate new detector signals
- Enhanced local processing (better ADC resolution, waveform digitization)
- Upgraded radio transmission capability
- Improved solar panels and batteries to power additional detectors

**Why**:
- Necessary to read out any new detectors
- Can improve timing resolution for better shower reconstruction
- Essential infrastructure

**Cost**: ~$1,500–2,000 per station

## 5. **Surface Array Timing Enhancement**

**Technology**:
- Replace or supplement existing GPS receivers with improved timing systems
- Better time resolution (<5 ns vs current ~10 ns)

**Why**:
- Improved shower geometry reconstruction
- Better arrival time patterns can provide some mass sensitivity
- Lower priority than direct muon counting

## **RECOMMENDED UPGRADE PACKAGE**

Given the constraints, the optimal proposal should include:

**Primary upgrade (all 1,660 stations)**:
- **Surface scintillator detectors** (3 m² per station): ~$5,000
- **Enhanced readout electronics and DAQ**: ~$1,000
- **Deployment labor and integration**: ~$200
- **Total**: ~$6,200 per station ✓

**Optional/subset deployments**:
- Underground muon detectors at ~300 strategically located stations for calibration
- Radio antennas at ~150 stations where RFI permits

This configuration provides:
- Direct muon measurement at every station
- Event-by-event mass sensitivity across full array
- 100% duty cycle operation
- Compatibility with existing data through unchanged water-Cherenkov response
- Proven, mature technology
- Feasible deployment timeline

TOP RECOMMENDATION: **Surface scintillator muon detectors (3 m² plastic scintillator modules with SiPM readout) installed adjacent to each water-Cherenkov station**

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Teral Plain Array

## Context Analysis

The instrument as described is essentially the Pierre Auger Observatory's water-Cherenkov detector array, adapted here with slightly different parameters. The core challenge is **muon/EM separation in a single-signal detector**, compounded by limited fluorescence duty cycle (12%). The 80–84° zenith angle ("inclined shower") strategy is clever because the EM component is attenuated by the extra atmosphere, leaving a muon-dominated signal — but this only works well near the edges of the array and sacrifices solid angle.

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Underground Muon Counters (Primary Recommendation)

**Technology:** Plastic scintillator slabs (e.g., 3×1 m Eljen EJ-200 tiles read by SiPMs) buried ~2.3 m underground beside each surface station, shielded by ~540 g/cm² of soil.

- At that depth, electromagnetic particles (electrons, low-energy photons) are fully absorbed; only muons with kinetic energy above ~160 MeV penetrate.
- Each underground unit provides a **direct muon count**, decoupled from the EM signal measured by the water-Cherenkov tank above.
- SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE, 6×6 mm, ~35% PDE) replace PMTs: they are compact, low-bias-voltage (50–70 V vs. ~1–2 kV), rugged, and require no high-voltage supply chain.
- A 3 m² scintillator area per station gives adequate muon counting statistics (expect ~5–50 muon hits per station per shower at 10^19 eV at relevant distances).
- Power budget: each underground unit draws ~0.5 W continuously (SiPM bias + FPGA readout), compatible with existing solar infrastructure with modest panel expansion (~10 W additional per station).
- Communication: underground unit connects via short-range 2.4 GHz link or buried cable to the surface station's existing radio uplink.
- **Muon number resolution gain:** Direct EM/muon decomposition at every station for every shower, every hour of operation — not just during inclined events. Expected resolution improvement to ~15–20% at 10^19.5 eV, well within the 30% requirement.

---

### 2. Surface Station PMT Upgrade to Dual-Threshold Fast Electronics

**Technology:** Replace current PMT readout boards with FPGA-based waveform digitizers (e.g., 12-bit, 250 MSPS ADC, similar to the ATCA-based systems used in upgraded Auger) with **100 ns time-over-threshold** discrimination at two independent thresholds.

- The existing two PMTs per station are retained but read out with full waveform capture (currently only peak + integral are typically stored).
- Full waveform allows **rise-time and late-muon-pulse** analysis: muon hits arrive as sharp, late pulses after the EM pancake; deconvolving the waveform partially separates muon contribution even in vertical showers.
- Specifically: fit each waveform to a sum of single-muon templates (narrow, ~15 ns FWHM Cherenkov pulse in 1.3 m water) and EM sub-threshold pile-up templates, using a maximum-likelihood estimator run on-board.
- FPGA (Xilinx Artix-7 or similar, ~1 W) stores 4 μs waveform windows per trigger, transmitted via existing radio link (adds ~2 kB per event per station, manageable at typical shower rates of ~1 Hz array-wide).
- **Cost:** ~$800/station for ADC + FPGA board replacement; $1.1M total for 1,350 stations.

---

### 3. Add a Third PMT Per Station, Oriented Laterally

**Technology:** A third 8-inch Hamamatsu R5912 PMT (or equivalent) mounted on the **side wall** of each polyethylene vessel, viewing horizontally through the water volume.

- The existing two PMTs view from above (downward-looking), predominantly sensitive to Cherenkov light from downward-going particles.
- A side-mounted PMT is geometrically more sensitive to **upward-going Cherenkov cones** produced by muons traversing the full 1.3 m water depth, distinguishing them from EM particles that stop or scatter near the surface.
- The asymmetry in top vs. side signal ratios provides an event-by-event EM/muon estimator without underground burial.
- Requires a waterproof feedthrough (existing designs used for Auger, e.g., Tetra Pak–style overmold) and modest pressure resistance (<0.2 bar at 1.3 m depth).
- **Power:** adds ~0.4 W per station (PMT HV supply).
- **Resolution contribution:** Monte Carlo studies on similar geometries suggest ~8% additional muon fraction resolution, complementary to upgrade #1.

---

### 4. Low-Power Radar Transponder Timing Upgrade

**Technology:** Replace or supplement the existing satellite timing (GPS 1 PPS, typical ~20 ns jitter) with **White Rabbit Ethernet timing over the radio link** (sub-nanosecond synchronization).

- Current 20 ns GPS timing jitter limits shower plane reconstruction accuracy at the array scale (0.7 km grid, timing baseline ~2.3 μs for a horizontal shower).
- White Rabbit (CERN-developed, IEEE 1588 PTPv2 extension) achieves <1 ns synchronization over fiber; a radio-adapted version using 900 MHz spread-spectrum links achieves ~3–5 ns.
- Improved timing tightens shower front geometry reconstruction, which directly improves **Xmax estimation from the array alone** (using shower front curvature and risetime methods), reducing dependence on the 12%-duty-cycle fluorescence telescopes.
- **Hardware:** replace current radio modem (e.g., existing 433 MHz modules) with 900 MHz White Rabbit radio nodes (prototype units ~$300 each; production cost ~$150).

---

### 5. Upgraded Fluorescence Telescopes: Hybrid EMCCD + SiPM Focal Plane

**Technology:** At the two existing fluorescence sites, replace photomultiplier camera pixels with **SiPM tile arrays** (e.g., SensL/OnSemi J-series 6×6 mm, tiled to match current ~40 mm pixel spacing).

- SiPMs offer ~50% PDE vs. ~25% for standard bialkali PMTs in the near-UV (300–400 nm fluorescence band).
- Doubles photon statistics per pixel → extends the fluorescence detection threshold downward by ~0.3 decades in energy, increasing the stereo Xmax calibration sample.
- More critically: **increases the duty cycle indirectly** by allowing operation under slightly elevated night-sky background (moon up to 30% illumination), potentially raising effective duty cycle from 12% to ~16–18%.
- SiPMs require active temperature stabilization (bias voltage tracks ~22 mV/°C on a high plateau); integrate a Dallas DS18B20 per tile with FPGA-controlled bias DAC per pixel row.
- **No structural telescope modification needed**; focal plane is a drop-in replacement.

---

### 6. Inter-Station Buried Scintillator Infill (Partial Deployment)

**Technology:** Deploy a subset (~200 units) of **1 m² × 5 cm thick plastic scintillator ground pads** (Fermilab-heritage Auger infill design) at triangle midpoints on a 350 m sub-grid in one 50 km² sector.

- Denser sampling in the infill region allows **direct measurement of the muon lateral distribution function (LDF)** shape, constraining hadronic interaction models.
- This provides a **calibration region** where the muon number estimator developed for inclined showers (80–84°) can be cross-checked against direct counting.
- Scintillator pads read by WLS fiber + SiPM (Kuraray Y-11 fiber, 2 m length to SiPM at pad edge), no PMT needed.
- Surface deployment (not underground) is acceptable for the calibration purpose since the muon LDF shape vs. EM is extracted statistically across many events.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Technology | Estimated Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| Underground scintillator muon counters | Direct μ/EM separation every shower | EJ-200 + SiPM + burial | ~$18M |
| Waveform digitizer upgrade | Pulse-shape μ/EM separation | 12-bit 250 MSPS FPGA board | ~$1.1M |
| Third lateral PMT per tank | Geometric μ/EM separation | R5912 + feedthrough | ~$2.7M |
| White Rabbit timing | Better Xmax from array alone | 900 MHz WR radio nodes | ~$0.2M |
| SiPM fluorescence focal plane | Higher duty cycle, better Xmax | SiPM tiles + bias control | ~$3M |
| Scintillator infill sector | Muon LDF calibration | WLS + SiPM ground pads | ~$1M |

---

## Critical Consideration on the 30% Resolution Requirement

At 10^19.5 eV, a typical inclined shower at 80° produces ~100 muon hits across O(100) stations. The statistical muon number uncertainty from pure counting is already ~10%. The 30% budget is dominated by **shower-to-shower fluctuations** (~20%) and **model uncertainty in muon production** (~15%). No hardware upgrade eliminates the latter — it requires cross-calibration with fluorescence Xmax data. Therefore the fluorescence SiPM upgrade (item 5) has outsized importance despite appearing secondary.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Deploy plastic scintillator muon detectors (EJ-200 slabs read by SiPMs) buried ~2.3 m underground beside each surface station, providing direct muon counts decoupled from the electromagnetic signal at every station for every shower in full-time operation.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Teral Plain Array

## The key physics constraint

The composition programme uses showers at 80–84° zenith. That choice changes which upgrade matters.

- **The ground signal is already mostly muons.** At these angles the shower crosses roughly 3,000–7,000 g/cm² of atmosphere before reaching the array. The electromagnetic cascade from the shower core is essentially absorbed. What reaches the water stations is mainly muons, plus a residual electromagnetic "halo" from muon decay of perhaps 10–20%, which can be modelled.
- **The existing stations are good muon detectors for this geometry.** Each 1.3 m deep, 11 m² water volume presents a large sidewall cross-section to near-horizontal muons. The ground footprint stretches to many km², so many stations are hit.
- **The missing measurement is the electromagnetic energy.** For inclined showers, the water stations' "single mixed signal" problem is largely solved by geometry. What is lacking is an independent, full-duty-cycle measurement of the electromagnetic component. Without it, the muon number cannot be separated from the primary energy, and composition cannot be inferred.

A common upgrade choice, flat scintillator panels on each station lid, is wrong here. A horizontal panel's projected area falls as cos θ, which is only about 0.10–0.17 at 80–84°. The panels would also see almost no electromagnetic particles, because those particles are absorbed before reaching the ground.

## 1. Radio antenna on every station (primary upgrade)

**Technology**
- Dual-polarised, wideband antenna in the 30–80 MHz band (SALLA or butterfly type), mounted on each station.
- Low-noise amplifiers, with digitisation at roughly 250 MHz or more.
- Powered from the station's existing solar system.
- Read out when the water station triggers, using the existing satellite timing and radio communications.

**Physics motivation**
- **It measures the electromagnetic energy directly.** The radio signal comes from geomagnetic and charge-excess emission by shower electrons and positrons. It is a calorimetric measure of the electromagnetic energy, accurate to about 10%, and the atmosphere is transparent to it.
- **It works almost all the time.** Unlike the fluorescence sites (about 12% of the time), radio operates close to 100% of the time, interrupted only by thunderstorms.
- **The array spacing suits inclined showers.** At 80–84° the radio footprint spans several km, so a 0.7 km grid samples it with many antennas. For vertical showers, radio footprints are too small for this spacing.
- **Together with the water stations, it gives both components for every event:**
  - radio supplies the electromagnetic energy;
  - the water stations supply the muon number, via fits of the measured muon density to a reference muon-density map.
  - The muon number at fixed electromagnetic energy then discriminates composition: iron produces about 40% more muons than protons.
- **It meets the resolution target.** A muon-number resolution of 30% or better at 10^19.5 eV is achievable when the energy is fixed independently to about 10%.
- **It adds a second composition handle.** Radio can also provide a depth-of-shower-maximum-sensitive observable.
- **It can be cross-calibrated against fluorescence** during the dark, clear nights when the fluorescence sites operate.

## 2. Upgraded station electronics

**Technology**
- Faster digitisation (at least 120 MHz) with higher-resolution analogue-to-digital converters.
- Improved satellite-timing receivers.
- A shared board that also digitises the radio channels.

**Physics motivation**
- Finer time traces allow individual muon pulses to be counted in far-from-core stations, and the decay-halo contribution to be fitted out.
- Better timing improves reconstruction of the arrival direction and shower-front curvature. This matters because zenith-angle errors near 80° change the atmospheric depth traversed strongly.
- Nanosecond-level synchronisation between stations allows interferometric radio reconstruction.

## 3. Small-dynamic-range photomultiplier in each water volume

**Technology**
- An additional small-area photomultiplier in each station, extending the dynamic range by about a factor of 30.

**Physics motivation**
- Near-core stations in high-energy events (above 10^19.5 eV) saturate.
- Unsaturated signals reduce the uncertainty in the muon-density fit and help keep resolution at or below 30% for the highest-energy events.

## 4. Optional: buried muon counters at a subset of stations

**Technology**
- Segmented scintillator counters buried under about 2.5 m of soil, at a small number of stations.

**Physics motivation**
- These are not needed for the inclined-shower programme itself.
- They provide a direct muon-counting cross-check of the water-station muon estimates and of the size of the electromagnetic halo correction.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a dual-polarised 30–80 MHz radio antenna on every station to measure the electromagnetic energy of inclined (80–84°) showers full-time, while the water stations supply the muon number.

# Hardware Upgrades for Muon/Electromagnetic Separation at the Teral Plain Array

## 1. Why the current stations cannot do this

The station is a 0.25 m deep water layer, which is only about 0.7 radiation lengths.

- **Muons:** a vertical muon crosses it and deposits about 50 MeV.
- **Electrons and photons:** shower electromagnetic particles of tens of MeV deposit a similar order of energy, so the electromagnetic and muon responses are only modestly different.
- **No fix from the top:** adding a thin scintillator on the lid (the AugerPrime-style surface scintillator) would give two detectors with nearly the same muon-to-electromagnetic response ratio. The two-detector matrix inversion would be almost singular, and muon-number resolution would be far worse than 30%.
- **No fix by adding water:** the tank cannot be deepened in place, because the water is already within 5 cm of the lid.

What is needed is a detector whose electromagnetic response is strongly suppressed relative to its muon response. That means one of two things:

- heavy shielding (a buried counter), or
- a separate deep water volume (more than 1 m), paired with a thin detector of very different response.

At 0–35° zenith, the electromagnetic component still dominates ground signals, so a shielded detector is the cleanest choice.

## 2. Primary upgrade: buried muon counters at every station (AMIGA-style)

**Detector**
- About 30 m² of segmented plastic scintillator per station.
- Configured as 3 × 10 m² modules of 64 strips each. Each strip is 4 m × 4.1 cm × 1 cm, extruded polystyrene with a TiO₂ coating.
- A wavelength-shifting fibre in each strip is read out by an array of silicon photomultipliers (Hamamatsu S13360-class, 1.3–1.4 mm pixels).

**Shielding**
- Buried at about 2.3 m depth, giving roughly 540 g/cm² of soil.
- This sets an electromagnetic cutoff and a muon threshold of about 1 GeV.
- At 0–35° zenith the slant overburden stays at 540–660 g/cm², which is ideal for this composition window.

**Placement**
- Each counter sits about 7–10 m from the station, outside the tank's shadow and clear of any punch-through from the tank.

**Readout**
- A binary counting mode, with per-strip discrimination and 3.125 ns sampling, avoids Poisson-plus-Landau fluctuations.
- An integrator mode extends the dynamic range near the shower core.

**Expected resolution**
- At 10^19.5 eV the shower footprint on the 0.7 km grid covers about 10–20 stations.
- At the reference distance of about 450 m, the muon density gives several hundred muons per 30 m² counter.
- This yields roughly 10–15% Poisson-plus-reconstruction resolution on N_µ, well inside the 30% target. Shower-to-shower fluctuations dominate, as they should.

**Cost-saving option**
- Use 10 m² counters on a 1.4 km sub-grid, with full 30 m² coverage only near infill areas.
- This should still meet 30% at 10^19.5 eV. Simulate it before committing.

## 3. Supporting upgrades

**Station electronics**
- Upgrade to 120 MHz, 14-bit FADCs, with a common GPS timing module (u-blox class, timing to 5 ns or better). This allows sub-trace timing so the muon "spikes" can be used.
- Add an extra small-area PMT (about 1 inch, roughly 1/30 the gain) to extend the dynamic range by more than 30×, avoiding saturation within about 300 m of the core.

**Power and communications**
- Add one more solar panel and battery for the counter's SiPM bias and electronics (about 1–2 W added).
- Upgrade the radio link bandwidth to carry the muon-counter traces.

**Monitoring**
- Use SiPM temperature compensation (bias feedback), since diurnal swings on high, dry grassland are large.
- Run continuous single-muon calibration with background muons.

**Cross-calibration**
- Use the fluorescence-detector hybrid nights, about 12% of the time, to calibrate N_µ against X_max and quantify the muon deficit seen in hadronic models.
- These nights provide the training set for the full-time composition estimator.

## 4. Alternatives considered and rejected

- **Surface scintillator on the lid:** almost the same response matrix as a 0.25 m water layer, so it is degenerate.
- **RPCs under the tank (MARTA-style):** only 0.25 m of water above them, so there is negligible electromagnetic shielding at 0–35° zenith.
- **Radio antennas:** they measure the electromagnetic energy well, but are most effective at high zenith angles and do not deliver a muon number.
- **Replacing all 1,350 vessels with 1.2 m deep water tanks plus a scintillator:** this is viable, but costs more than burial and gives poorer separation than shielding.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install ~30 m² SiPM-read segmented scintillator muon counters buried ~2.3 m deep beside every station, with upgraded station electronics, to count muons directly with the electromagnetic component absorbed.

## Design Review Recommendation for Pierre Auger Observatory Enhancement

### Physics Context
The key challenge is distinguishing proton-initiated showers (muon-poor) from iron-initiated showers (muon-rich) at ultra-high energies using the surface array alone. The electromagnetic component attenuates significantly by ground level, but muons penetrate effectively, creating a mass-sensitive signature if we can separate the two components.

### Recommended Hardware Addition: Underground Scintillator Muon Detectors

**Primary Recommendation: Add a buried scintillator module beside each water-Cherenkov station**

#### Specific Design:

1. **Scintillator Module Specifications:**
   - 2 modules per station, each 3 m × 1 m × 0.05 m plastic scintillator panel
   - Total area: 6 m² per station (compared to 10 m² water tank)
   - Buried at 2.3 m depth for electromagnetic shielding (equivalent to ~550 g/cm² soil)
   - Extruded polystyrene scintillator with wavelength-shifting fiber readout
   - Two 3-inch photomultipliers per station (one per panel)
   
2. **Installation Method:**
   - Excavate two trenches adjacent to existing station using compact excavator
   - Position scintillator modules in weatherproof sealed enclosures
   - Backfill with excavated soil
   - No disturbance to existing 12-tonne water station
   - Cable connection to existing station electronics enclosure

3. **Electronics Integration:**
   - Compact PMT base and preamp powered from existing solar system
   - Digital signal sent to existing station DAQ via short cable
   - GPS timestamp synchronized with existing station
   - Transmitted via existing radio link as additional data channel
   - Power consumption: ~3 W additional per station

#### Cost Breakdown (per station):
- Scintillator panels (6 m²): $1,800
- Two 3-inch PMTs and bases: $1,200
- Weatherproof enclosures: $600
- Electronics (digitizer, interface): $800
- Cable and connectors: $200
- Excavation equipment rental (amortized): $400
- Installation materials: $300
- Contingency (15%): $900
**Total: ~$6,200** ✓

#### Labor Breakdown (per station):
- Site preparation and marking: 0.5 hr
- Excavation (2 trenches): 2.0 hr
- Module placement and leveling: 1.0 hr
- Cable routing and connection: 1.5 hr
- Electronics checkout and calibration: 0.5 hr
- Backfilling and site restoration: 0.3 hr
**Total: ~5.8 person-hours** ✓

### Physics Performance:

**Muon Separation Capability:**
- At 2.3 m depth, electromagnetic component suppressed by factor >1000
- Muons above ~0.3 GeV penetrate efficiently
- Clean measurement of muonic component correlated with primary mass
- Signal in water tank minus signal in buried detector ≈ electromagnetic component

**Mass Discrimination:**
- Proton showers: muon fraction ~20% at ground level
- Iron showers: muon fraction ~40% at ground level  
- Two-component measurement enables event-by-event mass estimation
- Expected separation power: Δ⟨ln A⟩ ≈ 0.4-0.6 per event at 10^19.5 eV

### Alternative Considered but Rejected:

**Surface scintillator layers on top of tanks:**
- Lower cost (~$4,000/station)

**Deeper burial (>3 m):**
- Better EM suppression
- BUT: excavation costs exceed budget

2. **Proven technology:** Similar buried scintillators used successfully at Telescope Array
3. **Robust:** Sealed modules survive harsh Pampas environment
4. **Scalable deployment:** Modular installation fits field campaign schedule
5. **Immediate science:** Provides day-one mass discrimination capability
6. **100% duty cycle:** Operates continuously like water stations

### Implementation Strategy:

- Deploy in phases: 600 stations in year 1, 1,060 in year 2
- Prioritize central array (highest rate) first
- Factory pre-testing of all modules
- Two-person mobile installation teams with excavator support
- Real-time data quality monitoring during deployment

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Separating the EM and Muon Signals at Every Station

## 1. The physics problem and the lever

At fixed energy, an iron shower differs from a proton shower in two ways:
- it reaches maximum higher in the atmosphere (X_max is about 80–100 g/cm² shallower);
- it carries about 30–40% more muons at the ground.

Each water tank records one number that mixes both components. That number cannot tell the two primaries apart event by event.

The fix is to add a second detector at each station that responds to the two components in a **different ratio** from the water. A thin scintillator does this:
- Electrons, positrons and photons deposit relative to their number. The EM particle flux is about 10× the muon flux.
- Muons deposit only about 2 MeV, almost independent of their energy.
- The deep water tank, by contrast, is a calorimeter for the EM part and gives large track-length signals for muons.

Two detectors with different and well-known EM/μ response matrices let you solve, station by station, for the EM and muonic signals. From those you get:
- the muon content N_μ;
- X_max-sensitive observables, such as the shape of the EM lateral distribution and the rise time.

The scintillator sits **on top of** the tank. It therefore sees nearly the same particles and needs no access to the water volume.

## 2. Recommended upgrades, in priority order

### A. Surface Scintillator Detector (SSD) on every tank (core upgrade)

**Design**
- About 3.8 m² of extruded plastic scintillator, roughly 1 cm thick.
- Bars about 1.6 m × 5 cm, read out by wavelength-shifting fibres routed to a single 1.5-inch PMT.
- Housed in an aluminium light-tight box with a double roof (sun shield) to limit the daily temperature swing.

**Mounting**
- A galvanised steel frame bolts onto the existing tank lifting lugs and hatch area.
- It does **not** penetrate the liner or the water volume.
- The station response stays identical to the archived data.

**Physics reach**
- Matrix inversion of the water and scintillator signals at about 1 km from the core.
- N_μ resolution of about 15–20% at 10^19.5 eV for zenith angles below 60°.
- Combined with the water-tank rise time, this gives a merit factor above 1.5 for p/Fe separation. That is close to the event-by-event goal, at 100% duty cycle.

**Cost**
- About US$ 3,000–3,500 per unit, including scintillator, fibres, PMT, box, frame and cabling.

**Labour**
- Pre-assembled and tested in a central hall, then transported 2–4 per pickup on racks.
- Field mounting takes 2 people × about 1 h.
- Total: about 2–2.5 person-hours per station including travel share.

**Weight**
- About 150 kg. It is lifted by a small truck-mounted crane or hand-winch.
- The tank itself is never moved.

### B. Upgraded station electronics board (required to exploit A)

The new board replaces the existing electronics in the external electronics enclosure. Nothing inside the water is touched.

**Features**
- More input channels: 3 water-tank PMTs (high and low gain) plus the SSD PMT (high and low gain).
- Faster sampling: about 120 MHz and 12-bit, versus 40 MHz and 10-bit. This improves time-trace resolution, which helps muon/EM separation from trace shape (muon "spikes" against a smooth EM signal).
- An upgraded GPS receiver for better timing.
- A modern FPGA/CPU for new triggers.
- Spare inputs for future detectors.

**Dynamic range near the core**
- This is handled with an extra low-gain readout of the existing PMTs and the SSD's own dual gain.
- It does **not** require a new small PMT inserted into the tank, which would open the liner and break the "no alteration" rule.
- A dedicated small SSD PMT channel or attenuated dynode readout covers near-core saturation instead.

**Cost and labour**
- About US$ 1,500–2,000 per station.
- About 1 person-hour to swap, cable and commission. This can be done in the same visit as the SSD.

### C. Within-budget extras (optional, if margin remains)

**Radio antenna on the SSD frame**
- Cost: about US$ 500–700 per station, about 0.5 h to install.
- It measures the EM energy of inclined showers. That is mostly useful above 60°, so it is secondary to the stated goal. Its value is cross-calibration and future reach.

**Underground muon counters (about 30 m² buried 2.3 m deep)**
- These give a clean muon measurement but need excavation of tens of person-hours per station and cost well above budget.
- Deploy only on a small infill or engineering sub-array, for example 50–60 stations, to calibrate the SSD–water muon separation against direct muon counting.
- Do not deploy array-wide.

### Rejected options

| Option | Reason for rejection |
|---|---|
| Segmenting the tank or adding layers inside it | Violates the sealed-volume and liner constraint |
| Adding a PMT in a tank port | Violates the sealed-volume and liner constraint |
| Replacing or relocating tanks | Violates the no-lift, no-drain constraint |
| Lead or iron shielding over the tank | Changes the archived response, heavy, logistically prohibitive |

## 3. Budget and labour check (per station)

| Item | Cost (US$) | Person-hours |
|---|---|---|
| SSD (detector, frame, box) | ~3,300 | ~2.3 |
| Electronics board, cables, GPS | ~1,800 | ~1.0 |
| Shipping, deployment logistics, spares (~10%) | ~600 | — |
| Travel share / commissioning | — | ~1.2 |
| Radio antenna (optional) | ~500 | ~0.5 |
| **Total** | **~6,200** | **~5.0** |

Notes on the totals:
- The total of about US$ 6,200 includes the optional radio antenna. Without it the total is about US$ 5,700, leaving contingency.
- The total is within the 5.8 person-hour per station allowance.
- Combining SSD and electronics in **one visit per station** is what makes the labour fit.
- At about 6–8 stations per crew-day with 3–4 crews, the 18-month campaign is feasible.

## 4. Calibration and validation

- **Natural calibration:** the SSD is calibrated with atmospheric minimum-ionising muons (MIP histograms) from its own triggers, in the same way the tanks use vertical-equivalent muons.
- **Composition check:** cross-check the SSD and water composition observables against fluorescence X_max on the hybrid subset (15% duty cycle).
- **Muon-counting check:** cross-check against the buried muon counters on the infill.
- **Archive continuity:** the water-only reconstruction runs unchanged in parallel, so the archived data set stays continuous.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Mount a ~4 m² plastic scintillator detector on top of every water-Cherenkov tank, read out by upgraded faster electronics, so that the combined scintillator and water signals separate the electromagnetic and muonic components station by station.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Teral Plain Array

## Context and Core Problem

The fundamental challenge is separating muonic from electromagnetic (EM) components in a single-layer water Cherenkov detector. The current design cannot distinguish between a muon traversing the tank and an electron/photon depositing energy electromagnetically. Every proposed upgrade targets this separation.

---

## 1. Segmented Underground Muon Counters (Highest Priority)

**Proposal:** Bury a scintillator muon counter beneath each existing water Cherenkov station, at a depth of ~2.5 m of soil (~540 g/cm²).

**Specifics:**
- **Technology:** 3 m² of extruded polystyrene scintillator (EPS, e.g., Fermilab-style strips), 1 cm thick, with embedded wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers (Y-11 Kuraray, 1.0 mm diameter) read out by **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)** — specifically Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE or equivalent, 6×6 mm active area, ~50 µm pixel pitch.
- **Depth:** 2.5 m of overburden suppresses the EM shower particles by >99.9% while transmitting ~95% of vertical muons above 1 GeV.
- **Geometry:** Four 0.75 m² scintillator tiles per station in a 2×2 arrangement, each read by two WLS fibers routed to a single SiPM, providing crude multiplicity and hit-pattern information.
- **Power:** SiPM bias (~55 V) and readout draws <0.5 W per station, compatible with the existing solar power budget.
- **Timing:** Synchronize to the surface station's GPS timing via the existing radio link; require <10 ns coincidence window to tag genuine muon signals.
- **Expected gain:** Direct muon count at ground level, independent of EM flood, improving muon number resolution from ~50% toward the target 30% at 10^19.5 eV.
- **Cost driver:** Trenching and burial at 1,350 sites is the dominant cost, but the detector material itself is cheap (~$30/m² scintillator).

---

## 2. Segmented Water Cherenkov Layer with Optical Partition

**Proposal:** Retrofit the interior of each water tank with a horizontal Tyvek optical separator at a depth of 0.6 m, creating two independent optical volumes, each with its own PMT.

**Specifics:**
- **Material:** 0.6 m upper chamber and 0.7 m lower chamber, separated by a Tyvek 1082D diffuse-reflective partition with a central 0.1 m² hole allowing EM showers to develop but attenuating direct Cherenkov light transfer between layers.
- **PMTs:** Replace existing two-PMT configuration with four PMTs total — two 8-inch Hamamatsu R5912 (quantum efficiency ~25% at 400 nm) on the upper layer, two on the lower layer.
- **Principle:** An electron/photon generates most Cherenkov light near the entry point in the upper volume and is absorbed within ~0.3 radiation lengths of water (~20 cm). A relativistic muon deposits minimum-ionizing energy (~2 MeV/cm) uniformly through both layers. The ratio of lower-to-upper signal then provides a statistical EM/muon discriminant on a shower-by-shower basis.
- **Calibration:** Use vertical through-going muons (which give equal signals in both layers) for gain equalization.
- **Resolution contribution:** Roughly doubles the information content of each station for composition, reducing muon number uncertainty by ~√2 statistically across the shower footprint.

---

## 3. Radio Antenna Array for Shower Longitudinal Profile

**Proposal:** Co-locate a self-triggered radio antenna at each station to measure the coherent radio emission from the air shower.

**Specifics:**
- **Antenna type:** Butterfly/LPDA (log-periodic dipole antenna) dual-polarization, covering 30–80 MHz band — the **AERA/LOFAR** design heritage (e.g., as deployed at Auger's AERA extension).
- **Electronics:** A dedicated RF front-end board using a **LNA (low-noise amplifier)** with noise figure <1 dB (e.g., Mini-Circuits PSA4-5043+), bandpass filter (30–80 MHz), and 12-bit ADC at 200 MSa/s (e.g., Texas Instruments ADS4222).
- **Self-triggering:** Use a threshold trigger on the filtered RF envelope; cross-check with the particle detector trigger to eliminate RFI.
- **Physics gain:** Radio emission in the 30–80 MHz band is dominated by geomagnetic and Askaryan mechanisms; the radio lateral distribution function and spectral slope are sensitive to X_max (depth of shower maximum), providing a **continuous-duty complement to the fluorescence telescopes** (which operate only 12% of the time).
- **Deployment density:** Not all 1,350 stations are needed; a sub-array of **~100–200 stations** at the array core (more densely instrumented region) suffices to reconstruct radio X_max for most showers, since the radio footprint at 10^19 eV extends ~200–400 m from the shower axis.
- **X_max resolution achievable:** ~20–30 g/cm² based on AERA/Tunka-Rex performance, comparable to fluorescence resolution, but at 100% duty cycle.
- **Power:** Modern low-power RF chains can run on <2 W per station; feasible within the existing solar budget with minor panel/battery upgrades.

---

## 4. PMT Upgrade to High-QE MCP-PMTs or Large-Area SiPMs

**Proposal:** Replace the existing photomultipliers in the water Cherenkov stations with higher-quantum-efficiency detectors.

**Specifics:**
- **Option A — Large-area SiPMs:** Use tiled arrays of 6×6 mm SiPMs (Hamamatsu S13360 series or SensL J-series) covering a total active area of ~75 cm² per readout point, ganged into groups to match current PMT coverage. These offer QE ~40–50% (vs. ~25% for standard bialkali PMTs), low operating voltage (~55 V), no magnetic sensitivity, and superior single-photon resolution.
- **Option B — High-QE PMTs:** Hamamatsu R12860-HQE (20-inch) with super-bialkali photocathode, QE ~35% at 390 nm — a direct drop-in replacement for standard 8-inch or 9-inch PMTs with the same mechanical interface.
- **Physics impact:** Higher QE increases the number of detected photons per muon track by ~50–70%, improving the **single-station signal-to-noise ratio** and reducing the threshold energy for muon counting. This is particularly important for inclined showers (up to 35° zenith) where the EM component is more attenuated and clean muon identification improves.
- **Timing:** SiPMs offer transit time spread <0.2 ns (vs. ~1–2 ns for PMTs), improving shower front timing and hence angular reconstruction, which affects X_max estimation via hybrid reconstruction.

---

## 5. Upgrade Fluorescence Sites with Extended-Duty Telescopes

**Proposal:** Add non-imaging Cherenkov/fluorescence detectors ("FAMOUS"-style concentrators) at the two existing fluorescence sites to extend operational duty cycle.

**Specifics:**
- **Technology:** Fresnel lens concentrators (1 m² aperture, f/1.0) coupled to SiPM focal-plane cameras (e.g., 61-pixel SiPM camera as in the FAMOUS telescope, Aachen design). Operating wavelength 300–420 nm (fluorescence + near-UV Cherenkov).
- **Advantage over classical FD:** SiPM-based telescopes can operate at moonlight levels up to ~30% lunar illumination without gain damage, increasing duty cycle from 12% to roughly **20–25%**.
- **Additional use:** Measure Cherenkov-to-fluorescence ratio for better energy calibration and X_max resolution (~15–20 g/cm²).
- **Number:** 3–4 Schmidt-telescope modules per site, covering overlapping fields of view over the central array.

---

## 6. Muon Tracking Capability via Resistive Plate Chambers (RPC)

**Proposal:** At a subset of ~50 "super-stations" (one per ~11 km²), deploy a stack of RPCs for 3D muon tracking.

**Specifics:**
- **Technology:** Four layers of single-gap glass RPCs (1.6 mm gap, 2 mm float glass), each 2 m × 2 m, stacked vertically with 30 cm spacing, operated in avalanche mode with an HV of ~5.5 kV.
- **Gas mixture:** C₂H₂F₄/Iso-C₄H₁₀/SF₆ (96.7/3/0.3%) — standard for ALICE/ATLAS-style RPCs, well-characterized and low-cost to operate.
- **Strip readout:** 1.7 cm copper strip pitch, read out by front-end ASICs (e.g., FERIX-3 or similar), giving ~1 cm spatial resolution per layer.
- **Physics:** Track individual muons, measure muon arrival angle and lateral distribution. The muon lateral distribution function (MLDF) at large distances (>500 m) from the core is particularly sensitive to composition (iron vs. proton) and is poorly measured by integrated-signal detectors.
- **Power/logistics:** RPCs require a gas system; at 50 sites, a central gas mixing/distribution system using small cylinders refilled annually is feasible.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Muon/EM separation | X_max info | Duty cycle | Complexity | Cost tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Buried scintillator muon counter | ★★★★★ | — | 100% | Medium | Medium |
| Segmented tank optical layer | ★★★ | — | 100% | Low | Low |
| Radio antenna sub-array | ★ (indirect) | ★★★★ | ~100% | Medium | Medium |
| High-QE PMT/SiPM upgrade | ★★ | ★ | 100% | Low | Low-Med |
| SiPM fluorescence telescopes | — | ★★★★ | +~10% | Medium | Medium |
| RPC super-stations (50 sites) | ★★★★ | — | 100% | High | High |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Bury a 3 m² SiPM-read scintillator muon counter at 2.5 m depth beneath every water Cherenkov station, providing a direct, continuous, shower-by-shower muon count independent of the electromagnetic component.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Teral Plain Array

## Context and Core Problem

The fundamental challenge is separating muonic from electromagnetic (EM) components in a single mixed signal per station. Everything below addresses this directly or supports it.

---

## 1. Muon/EM Separation: Underground Muon Detectors (UMDs)

**The most critical upgrade.**

Bury scintillator panels beneath each surface station at a depth of ~2.3 m of soil equivalent (~540 g/cm²). This shielding attenuates EM shower components by a factor >10⁵ while transmitting ~95% of muons above ~1 GeV.

- **Technology:** 3 mm thick extruded plastic scintillator strips (same as used in NOvA/MINERvA), wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber readout (Kuraray Y-11), silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs, e.g. Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE or KETEK PE6035)
- **Panel area:** 3 × 3 m² (9 m²) per station, one panel per station initially; optionally two panels offset for muon directionality
- **Electronics:** Triggered by coincidence with surface signal to suppress thermal noise; 12-bit 120 MSPS FADCs for waveform digitization
- **Power:** SiPMs draw ~1 mW bias current; full electronics ~3–5 W per station, achievable with existing solar budget if panels are upgraded (see §6)
- **Impact:** Provides a direct, independent muon count per station rather than a statistical inversion. Demonstrated viable at smaller scale in the AMIGA sub-array of Auger.

---

## 2. Surface Station Segmentation for EM/Muon Discrimination

If underground detectors are too costly for all 1,350 stations, segment the surface water-Cherenkov detector (WCD) signal using a layered scintillator-on-top approach.

- **Technology:** Place a 1 cm thick plastic scintillator tile (Saint-Gobain BC-408 or equivalent) on the lid of each WCD, read out by 4 SiPMs at corners. The scintillator sees EM + muon; the WCD signal below is normalized to subtract → muon-enriched residual.
- **Drawback:** Separation is statistical, not event-by-event at particle level. Achieves ~40–50% muon purity per station, insufficient alone but combined with shower geometry fits improves composition resolution.
- **Cost:** ~$400/station in scintillator + SiPMs at volume pricing.

---

## 3. Radio Antenna Arrays for Electromagnetic Shower Maximum (Xmax)

Replace 88% of fluorescence duty cycle loss with continuous radio measurement of Xmax.

- **Technology:** Dual-polarization log-periodic dipole antennas (LPDAs) in the 30–80 MHz band (same band as AERA/Auger and Tunka-Rex), one per station or one per cluster of 7 stations
- **Specific hardware:** LPDA arms ~1.2 m, low-noise amplifier (LNA) with noise figure <1 dB (e.g., Mini-Circuits PSA4-5043+ MMIC), 14-bit 200 MSPS ADC, FPGA-based trigger (Xilinx Artix-7), GPS white-rabbit timing to <2 ns
- **Bandwidth:** 30–80 MHz captures geomagnetic and charge-excess emission; beam-forming across array reconstructs Xmax to ~20 g/cm² RMS at 10^19 eV (demonstrated by AERA)
- **Data:** ~10 MB/event compressed; transmit only triggered windows over existing radio link
- **Duty cycle:** ~95% (limited only by RFI events, thunderstorms), vs. 12% for fluorescence
- **Impact:** Direct Xmax measurement full-time, enabling mass composition without relying on muon number alone; cross-calibration with fluorescence on 12% overlap sample

---

## 4. Improved Photomultiplier Replacement with SiPMs

Replace the two PMTs per station with SiPM arrays.

- **Technology:** 4 × 4 array of 6 mm × 6 mm SiPMs (Hamamatsu S13361-6050AE-04 or SensL J-series 60035), total active area ~9 cm² per unit, two units per station
- **Advantages over PMTs:**
  - No high-voltage supply (operate at 24–28 V bias)
  - Insensitive to magnetic field (irrelevant here but robust)
